etymology.story: The word frons also gave us "front" and "confront": the face you present to the world.

info.explanation: Single bone forming the forehead, the roof of the orbits and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa.

facts.function: Protects the frontal lobes; forms the forehead and the orbital roofs.
facts.lesion: Fracture of the anterior cranial fossa floor can tear the olfactory fibres (anosmia) and cause CSF rhinorrhoea.
facts.connections: Meets the parietals at the coronal suture.

etymology.story: The temples are where grey hair first shows, so the region marked the passing of time; tempus gave "temporal" and "temporary".

info.explanation: Paired bone on the side of the skull base housing the ear, with the squamous part forming the temple and a petrous part forming part of the middle and posterior fossae.

facts.function: Protects the temporal lobe; houses the middle and inner ear and carries the facial nerve canal and internal acoustic meatus.
facts.passes: Internal acoustic meatus carries CN VII and CN VIII; carotid canal carries the internal carotid artery.
facts.lesion: Thin squamous part overlies the middle meningeal artery: a fracture here classically causes an epidural haematoma. Petrous fracture can injure CN VII/VIII.

info.review_note: "Temple = where hair greys first" is the traditional explanation of tempus.

etymology.literal: bone at the back of the head
etymology.story: Occiput literally means "back of the head", the part behind (ob) the head (caput).

info.explanation: Single bone forming the back and base of the skull, containing the foramen magnum.

facts.function: Protects the occipital lobes and cerebellum; transmits the brainstem-spinal cord junction through the foramen magnum and articulates with the atlas.
facts.passes: Foramen magnum (medulla, vertebral arteries, spinal accessory roots); hypoglossal canal (CN XII).

etymology.story: Paries is the wall of a house; the two parietals form the side walls and roof of the cranial vault, and "parietal" also gave "parietal cells" and "college parietals".

info.explanation: Paired flat bones forming most of the roof and sides of the skull between the frontal and occipital bones.

facts.function: Protects the parietal lobes and forms the cranial vault.

etymology.story: It is wedged between the other skull bones like a bat or a butterfly, with the body, greater and lesser wings.

info.explanation: Complex midline bone in the skull base with a body (housing the sphenoid sinus and the pituitary fossa), greater and lesser wings, and pterygoid processes.

facts.function: Forms the floor of the middle cranial fossa and houses the pituitary gland in the sella turcica.
facts.passes: Optic canal (CN II, ophthalmic artery); superior orbital fissure (CN III, IV, V1, VI); foramen rotundum (V2); foramen ovale (V3); foramen spinosum (middle meningeal artery).

etymology.story: The suture runs straight front to back like the shaft of an arrow; sutura comes from suere, "to sew", the same root as "suture" in surgery.

info.explanation: Midline fibrous joint between the two parietal bones, running front to back along the top of the skull.

facts.function: Fibrous joint that allows skull growth in infancy, then fuses.
facts.lesion: Premature fusion (craniosynostosis) gives a long narrow skull (scaphocephaly).

etymology.story: Shaped like the capital Greek letter lambda (Λ) when seen from behind.

info.explanation: Fibrous joint between the occipital bone and the two parietal bones at the back of the skull.

facts.function: Fibrous joint permitting skull growth.

etymology.story: It runs over the head like the band of a crown (corona, from Greek korone, "something curved").

info.explanation: Fibrous joint between the frontal bone and the two parietal bones, running ear to ear across the top of the skull.

facts.function: Fibrous joint permitting skull growth.
facts.lesion: Premature closure produces a short, tall skull (brachycephaly).

etymology.story: Bregma is the Greek word for the front of the head; in infants it is the soft spot where the anterior fontanelle closes.

info.explanation: Point where the coronal and sagittal sutures meet; the site of the anterior fontanelle in infants.

facts.function: Surface landmark for neurosurgical approaches; the infant anterior fontanelle closes around 18 months.
facts.lesion: A bulging fontanelle indicates raised intracranial pressure; a sunken one dehydration.

etymology.story: Named because the sagittal and lambdoid sutures meet in a shape like the Greek letter lambda.

info.explanation: Point where the sagittal suture meets the two limbs of the lambdoid suture at the back of the skull; the site of the posterior fontanelle in infants.

facts.function: Surface landmark; the posterior fontanelle closes by about 2 months.

etymology.story: Named for its relation to the greater wing of the sphenoid (Greek pteron, "wing", as in "pterodactyl", wing-finger).

info.explanation: H-shaped junction of the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones on the side of the skull; the thinnest part of the lateral skull.

facts.function: Landmark overlying the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.
facts.supply: Anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery lies just deep to it.
facts.lesion: A blow here can fracture the bone and tear the middle meningeal artery, causing an epidural (extradural) haematoma.

etymology.story: Literally "the great hole", the largest opening in the skull.

info.explanation: Large opening in the occipital bone through which the medulla continues as the spinal cord.

facts.function: Passage between the cranial cavity and vertebral canal.
facts.passes: Medulla/spinal cord junction, vertebral arteries, spinal roots of CN XI, meninges.
facts.supply: Vertebral arteries enter here to form the basilar artery.
facts.lesion: Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through it compresses the medulla (respiratory and cardiac failure).

etymology.story: A fossa is a ditch: the cranial floor is stepped into three shallow ditches holding the frontal lobes, temporal lobes and cerebellum from front to back.

info.explanation: Shallowest and most rostral of the three cranial fossae, formed by the frontal bone, ethmoid and lesser wing of the sphenoid.

facts.function: Houses the frontal lobes and olfactory bulbs.
facts.passes: Cribriform plate transmits the olfactory nerve fibres (CN I).
facts.lesion: Fracture through the cribriform plate causes anosmia, CSF leak from the nose and "raccoon eyes".

etymology.story: The middle ditch in the stepped floor of the skull; its butterfly shape is created by the sphenoid and temporal bones.

info.explanation: Butterfly-shaped fossa formed by the sphenoid and temporal bones; the pituitary sits in its midline sella turcica.

facts.function: Houses the temporal lobes and the pituitary gland.
facts.passes: Optic canal (CN II), superior orbital fissure (III, IV, V1, VI), foramen rotundum (V2), foramen ovale (V3), foramen spinosum (middle meningeal a.).
facts.supply: Middle meningeal artery grooves its lateral wall.
facts.lesion: Basilar skull fracture here may injure cranial nerves or carotid artery.

etymology.story: The deepest of the three stepped ditches; posterior comes from post, "after, behind".

info.explanation: Deepest, most caudal fossa formed mainly by the occipital and temporal bones; the tentorium cerebelli forms its roof.

facts.function: Houses the cerebellum, pons and medulla.
facts.passes: Foramen magnum, internal acoustic meatus (VII, VIII), jugular foramen (IX, X, XI), hypoglossal canal (XII).
facts.lesion: Mass lesions here can obstruct the fourth ventricle (obstructive hydrocephalus) or herniate through the foramen magnum.

lists.note: Dura, Arachnoid and Pia layers of meninges

etymology.story: Medieval Latin rendering of Arabic phrases meaning "tough mother" and "tender mother" (dura and pia mater), because the membranes were thought to give rise to all other membranes of the body.

info.explanation: Thick outer meningeal layer with periosteal and meningeal layers that separate to form the dural venous sinuses.

facts.function: Protects and supports the brain; forms the falx and tentorium and houses the dural venous sinuses.
facts.supply: Meningeal arteries, chiefly the middle meningeal artery (from the maxillary artery); sensory supply from the trigeminal nerve.
facts.lesion: Epidural haematoma (middle meningeal a.) between bone and dura; subdural haematoma from torn bridging veins beneath it.

info.review_note: Arabic "mother" origin of dura/pia mater is the standard account.

etymology.story: The sickle-shaped fold of dura dividing the hemispheres; falx is the same word as a farmer's sickle (and "falcon" is related to the curved claw).

info.explanation: Sickle-shaped midline fold of dura mater in the longitudinal fissure between the two cerebral hemispheres.

facts.function: Separates and stabilises the cerebral hemispheres; carries the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses.
facts.lesion: Subfalcine herniation of the cingulate gyrus beneath it compresses the anterior cerebral artery.

etymology.story: From tendere, "to stretch", as in a stretched-canvas tent: the dural tent roofing the cerebellum.

info.explanation: Dural sheet stretched between the occipital lobes and the cerebellum, separating the supratentorial from infratentorial compartments.

facts.function: Supports the occipital lobes and separates them from the cerebellum; carries the transverse and straight sinuses.
facts.passes: The midbrain passes through the tentorial notch.
facts.lesion: Uncal herniation through the notch compresses CN III and the midbrain; bleeding "above vs below the tentorium" is a classic localiser.

lists.note: Dura, Arachnoid and Pia layers of meninges

etymology.story: Its delicate trabeculae resemble a spider's web, as in Greek arachne, the weaver turned into a spider in Ovid's tale.

info.explanation: Thin, avascular middle meningeal layer lying against the dura, with trabeculae crossing the subarachnoid space to the pia.

facts.function: Forms the barrier layer of the meninges and encloses the CSF-filled subarachnoid space; arachnoid granulations drain CSF.
facts.lesion: Subarachnoid haemorrhage from ruptured berry aneurysms; meningitis involves the arachnoid and pia.

lists.note: Dura, Arachnoid and Pia layers of meninges

etymology.story: The delicate counterpart to the "tough mother" (dura): pia means tender or gentle.

info.explanation: Thin, vascular innermost meningeal layer closely applied to the surface of the brain and spinal cord, following every sulcus.

facts.function: Supports the vessels entering the brain and forms the perivascular spaces.

etymology.story: Epi, "upon", as in epidermis, "upon the skin".

info.explanation: Potential space between the skull and dura in the cranium, and a real fat- and vein-filled space around the spinal dural sac.

facts.function: In the cranium it is only a potential space; in the spinal canal it is the site of epidural anaesthesia.
facts.lesion: Arterial (middle meningeal) bleed causes an epidural haematoma, lens-shaped on CT, with a lucid interval.

etymology.story: Sub, "under", the layer beneath the dura.

info.explanation: Potential space between the dura and arachnoid, actually a weak cell layer (dural border cell layer).

facts.function: Normally collapsed; bleeding can open it.
facts.supply: Bridging veins cross it to reach the dural sinuses.
facts.lesion: Torn bridging veins cause subdural haematoma, crescent-shaped on CT, common in the elderly, alcoholics and shaken infants.

etymology.story: The CSF-filled space under the arachnoid, traversed by web-like trabeculae.

info.explanation: CSF-filled space between arachnoid and pia containing the major cerebral arteries and veins.

facts.function: Cushions the CNS in CSF and carries the arteries of the circle of Willis.
facts.supply: Contains the circle of Willis and cerebral arteries.
facts.lesion: Subarachnoid haemorrhage (ruptured berry aneurysm) gives thunderclap headache and blood in CSF. Lumbar cistern is the site of lumbar puncture.

etymology.story: Meninx is the Greek word for membrane, giving "meningitis".

info.explanation: Vessels supplying the dura, chiefly the middle meningeal artery and its branches, with accompanying veins.

facts.function: Supply the dura and skull; run in grooves on the inner skull surface.
facts.supply: Middle meningeal artery arises from the maxillary artery and enters through the foramen spinosum.
facts.lesion: Rupture produces epidural haematoma.

etymology.story: Cerebrum is Latin for brain, from a root meaning "head"; the vessels lie in the subarachnoid space on the brain surface.

info.explanation: Arteries and veins visible on the brain surface within the subarachnoid space, comprising anterior and posterior circulations.

facts.function: Deliver oxygenated blood to and drain blood from the brain.
facts.supply: Internal carotid (anterior circulation) and vertebral-basilar (posterior circulation) arteries.
facts.lesion: Aneurysm rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage; occlusion causes ischaemic stroke.

etymology.story: Cortex means bark or rind, just like the bark of a tree: the thin grey outer layer.

info.explanation: Thin outer sheet of grey matter of the cerebral hemispheres, folded into gyri and sulci; mostly six-layered neocortex.

facts.function: Higher-order sensory processing, voluntary movement, language, memory and executive control.
facts.supply: Branches of the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries.
facts.lesion: Depends on location: stroke, aphasia, neglect, visual field loss.
facts.connections: Thalamocortical, corticocortical and corticofugal connections.

etymology.story: Called a stem because the hemispheres and cerebellum branch from it like a plant on a stalk. Latin truncus means trunk.

info.explanation: Midbrain, pons and medulla connecting the cerebrum and cerebellum to the spinal cord.

facts.function: Conduit for ascending and descending tracts; houses cranial nerve nuclei III-XII and the reticular formation that regulates arousal, breathing and heart rate.
facts.passes: Corticospinal, medial lemniscus, spinothalamic tracts and cerebellar peduncles.
facts.lesion: Brainstem stroke causes crossed signs: ipsilateral cranial nerve deficit with contralateral body deficit.

lists.group: Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus

etymology.story: Latin diminutive: "little brain", since it looks like a small brain tucked beneath the occipital lobes.

info.explanation: Structure behind the pons and medulla in the posterior fossa, with a midline vermis and two hemispheres.

facts.function: Coordinates movement, balance and motor learning on the same side of the body.
facts.passes: Three cerebellar peduncles connect it to the brainstem.
facts.supply: Superior cerebellar, AICA and PICA (vertebral/basilar branches).
facts.lesion: Ipsilateral ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor and nystagmus.
facts.connections: Output via deep cerebellar nuclei.

etymology.story: From ante, "before", the same prefix as in "antechamber".

info.explanation: Toward the front of the body; in the human it is equivalent to ventral, but in the neuraxis it is not equal to rostral.

etymology.story: From post, "after", as in "postpone".

info.explanation: Toward the back of the body; equivalent to dorsal in the human body.

etymology.story: Comparative of superus ("above"), also giving "superior" in rank.

info.explanation: Toward the top of the head; above.

etymology.story: From inferus, "below"; "inferno" is the underworld below.

info.explanation: Toward the feet; below.

etymology.story: Rostrum, a bird's beak or the prow of a ship; in the neuraxis rostral points toward the front of the head.

info.explanation: Toward the nose/front of the head along the neuraxis.

etymology.story: Cauda is Latin for tail, as in "coda" in music; caudal means toward the tail end.

info.explanation: Toward the tail end of the neuraxis (the sacral cord).

etymology.story: Dorsum is the back; "endorse" literally means to write on the back of a document.

info.explanation: Toward the back (spinal side) of the body or the top of the brainstem and spinal cord.

etymology.story: Venter is the belly; "ventriloquist" literally means "belly-speaker".

info.explanation: Toward the belly side of the body; the front of the brainstem and spinal cord.

etymology.story: From latus, "side", as in "bilateral".

info.explanation: Away from the midline.

etymology.story: From medius, "middle".

info.explanation: Toward the midline.

etymology.story: Same root as medial: median means in the exact midline.

info.explanation: In the midsagittal midline.

etymology.story: Facies means face or surface; superficial things lie "above the face" of an object.

info.explanation: Closer to the surface.

etymology.story: Latin profundus, "bottomless", gives "profound".

info.explanation: Farther from the surface.

etymology.story: The sagittal suture looked like an arrow shot from front to back, and the plane follows that direction.

info.explanation: Vertical plane running front to back, dividing the body into left and right parts; the midsagittal plane passes through the midline.

etymology.story: The plane runs parallel to the coronal suture, the line of a crown across the head.

info.explanation: Vertical plane dividing the body into anterior and posterior parts, parallel to the face.

etymology.story: Parallel to the horizon: from Greek horizein "to bound". Also called axial or transverse.

info.explanation: Plane dividing the body into upper and lower parts.

name: Neuraxis
synonyms: longitudinal axis of the nervous system

lists.note: Longitudinal axis of the nervous system (neuraxis)

etymology.story: Neuron originally meant sinew or cord in Greek, later nerve. The neuraxis is the long axis of the CNS.

info.explanation: Imaginary long axis of the central nervous system, running from the spinal cord to the forebrain; it bends at the midbrain flexure.

name: Orientation of the neuraxis (cerebrum vs brainstem/spinal cord)

lists.note: Orientation of neuraxis in the cerebrum vs. brainstem/spinal cord

roots.meaning: CNS long axis (O) axis of the central nervous system

etymology.story: The CNS axis bends at the midbrain, so the same word (e.g. dorsal) points in different directions in the cerebrum and the brainstem.

info.explanation: Because of the cephalic flexure, rostral-caudal and dorsal-ventral directions in the forebrain are rotated about 80-90 degrees relative to the brainstem and spinal cord.

etymology.story: The embryonic neural tube bends sharply at the midbrain (the mesencephalon, the "middle brain"), which is why the forebrain axis ends up tilted about 90 degrees to the brainstem and spinal cord.

info.explanation: Bend in the embryonic neuraxis at the midbrain that rotates the forebrain axis about 90 degrees relative to the brainstem.

etymology.story: Ventriculus is a diminutive of venter, "belly": a little belly or chamber, the same word used for the ventricles of the heart.

info.explanation: C-shaped CSF-filled cavity within each cerebral hemisphere, with frontal (anterior) horn, body, atrium, occipital (posterior) and temporal (inferior) horns.

facts.function: Contains choroid plexus that produces CSF; CSF drains to the third ventricle through the foramen of Monro.
facts.lesion: Blockage at the foramen of Monro or aqueduct causes obstructive hydrocephalus; enlargement ex vacuo follows tissue loss.
facts.connections: Communicates with the third ventricle via the interventricular foramen.

name: Anterior horn of lateral ventricle
synonyms: anterior horn of the lateral ventricle

etymology.story: Cornu is Latin for horn (hence "cornucopia", horn of plenty and "unicorn").

info.explanation: Part of the lateral ventricle in the frontal lobe, anterior to the foramen of Monro; its lateral wall is the head of the caudate and the medial wall the septum pellucidum.

facts.function: CSF space.
facts.connections: Bounded by the corpus callosum genu anteriorly and the caudate head laterally.

etymology.story: The TA calls it the central part; it runs beneath the body of the corpus callosum, whose name comes from Latin corpus, "body" (as in "corpse").

info.explanation: Part of the lateral ventricle under the body of the corpus callosum, with the caudate body laterally, thalamus inferiorly and fornix medially.

facts.function: CSF space.
facts.connections: Roof formed by the corpus callosum, floor by the thalamus and body of the caudate.

name: Inferior horn of lateral ventricle
synonyms: inferior horn of the lateral ventricle

etymology.story: Cornu, "horn", sweeping into the temporal lobe.

info.explanation: Curves from the atrium into the temporal lobe, with the hippocampus in its floor and the tail of the caudate in its roof.

facts.function: CSF space; choroid plexus runs in its choroid fissure.
facts.lesion: Enlarged temporal horns are an early sign of hydrocephalus or hippocampal atrophy.
facts.connections: Hippocampus forms its medial floor.

name: Posterior horn of lateral ventricle
synonyms: posterior horn of the lateral ventricle

etymology.story: Horn in the occipital lobe, "occipital" from ob + caput.

info.explanation: Extends from the atrium into the occipital lobe; no choroid plexus.

facts.function: CSF space.
facts.connections: Optic radiations lie lateral to it.

etymology.story: In a Roman house the atrium was the central hall from which rooms branch; here it is the junction of body, occipital and temporal horns.

info.explanation: Triangular junction of the body and the posterior and inferior horns, also called the trigone; contains a large tuft of choroid plexus (glomus).

facts.function: CSF space where choroid plexus is bulkiest.
facts.lesion: Calcification of the choroid glomus is a common normal finding on CT; CSF is trapped here in intraventricular haemorrhage.

lists.note: Septum pellucidum which separates the two lateral ventricles

etymology.story: Per (through) + lucere (to shine): it is thin enough to let light through, like "translucent".

info.explanation: Thin midline membrane of glia and white matter separating the two lateral ventricles between the corpus callosum and fornix.

facts.function: Separates the lateral ventricles.
facts.lesion: A cavum septum pellucidum is a common developmental variant; absence suggests midline defects.
facts.connections: Between the corpus callosum above and the fornix below.

etymology.story: Named for Alexander Monro secundus (1733-1817), the Edinburgh anatomist who described it.

info.explanation: Paired openings connecting each lateral ventricle with the third ventricle, bounded by the fornix and anterior thalamus.

facts.function: Allow CSF to flow from the lateral to the third ventricle.
facts.passes: CSF; choroid plexus is continuous through it.
facts.lesion: Obstruction (colloid cyst) causes unilateral/bilateral lateral ventricle dilation.

etymology.story: Counted third in the series of ventricles (two lateral ventricles are numbered first and second).

info.explanation: Narrow midline slit-like cavity between the two thalami and hypothalami.

facts.function: Passage of CSF from the lateral ventricles to the aqueduct.
facts.lesion: Colloid cyst can block it and cause hydrocephalus.
facts.connections: Connects to the lateral ventricles (foramina of Monro) and fourth ventricle (cerebral aqueduct).

lists.group: Rostral Midbrain – Level of Superior Colliculus
Caudal Midbrain – Level of Inferior Colliculus

etymology.story: "Aqueduct" is the Roman water channel; the aqueduct of Sylvius (named for Franciscus Sylvius) carries CSF through the midbrain.

info.explanation: Narrow canal through the midbrain connecting the third and fourth ventricles.

facts.function: Passage of CSF between the third and fourth ventricle.
facts.lesion: Stenosis causes obstructive hydrocephalus with enlarged lateral and third ventricles but a normal fourth ventricle.
facts.connections: Surrounded by the periaqueductal grey.

info.review_note: Sylvius attribution (Franciscus de le Boe) is conventional but debated.

lists.group: Rostral Pons – Level of Trigeminal Nerve
Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus

etymology.story: The fourth ventricle follows the numbering from the two laterals and the third.

info.explanation: Diamond-shaped cavity between the pons/medulla and cerebellum; continuous with the central canal of the medulla.

facts.function: Passes CSF into the subarachnoid space via the foramen of Magendie and the foramina of Luschka.
facts.lesion: Tumours (e.g. medulloblastoma, ependymoma) can block it; the floor is the rhomboid fossa with the facial colliculi.
facts.connections: Floor is the rhomboid fossa.

lists.note: Foramina of Magendie and Luschka (medial and lateral apertures)

etymology.story: Named for the French physiologist Francois Magendie (1783-1855).

info.explanation: Median aperture in the roof of the fourth ventricle that opens into the subarachnoid space (cisterna magna).

facts.function: Exit for CSF from the fourth ventricle at the midline.
facts.lesion: Blockage (e.g. Dandy-Walker malformation, post-infectious) causes hydrocephalus.

lists.note: Foramina of Magendie and Luschka (medial and lateral apertures)

etymology.story: Named after the German anatomist Hubert von Luschka (1820-1875).

info.explanation: Paired lateral apertures at the lateral recesses of the fourth ventricle that open into the subarachnoid space at the cerebellopontine angle.

facts.function: Exit for CSF from the fourth ventricle.
facts.lesion: Obstruction causes hydrocephalus; choroid plexus often protrudes through them.

etymology.story: Resembles the chorion, the fetal membrane, because of its vascular frond shape; plexus means "plaited" or "woven", as in "complex".

info.explanation: Vascular frond of capillaries covered by ependymal epithelium in the lateral, third and fourth ventricles.

facts.function: Produces CSF (~500 ml/day) and forms the blood-CSF barrier.
facts.lesion: Choroid plexus papilloma overproduces CSF; its hypersecretion can cause hydrocephalus.

etymology.story: Granulum is diminutive of granum, "grain", because they look like tiny grains.

info.explanation: Tufts of arachnoid that project into the dural venous sinuses, mainly the superior sagittal sinus.

facts.function: Reabsorb CSF into the venous blood.
facts.lesion: Impaired absorption (e.g. after subarachnoid haemorrhage or infection) causes communicating hydrocephalus.

etymology.story: Sinus means a curve or hollow; the sagittal sinus runs front to back like the sagittal suture beneath which it lies.

info.explanation: Midline dural venous sinus in the attached margin of the falx cerebri along the vault.

facts.function: Drains cerebral veins and CSF (via arachnoid granulations), eventually into the confluence of sinuses.
facts.supply: Drains superficial cerebral veins; CSF returns via granulations.
facts.lesion: Thrombosis causes venous infarction, seizures and raised intracranial pressure.

etymology.story: Callus is the same root: callosum means hard or thick-skinned, the early anatomists saw it as a tough bridge.

info.explanation: Largest commissure, connecting the two cerebral hemispheres; has rostrum, genu, body and splenium.

facts.function: Transfers information between the hemispheres.
facts.passes: Commissural fibres (e.g., fibres of the forceps minor and major).
facts.supply: Pericallosal and callosomarginal branches of the anterior cerebral artery; splenium also from posterior cerebral artery.
facts.lesion: Agenesis (ACC) and callosotomy cause disconnection syndromes (split-brain).
facts.connections: Connects homologous cortical areas.

etymology.story: Ganglion originally meant a swelling or knot under the skin; the basal ganglia lie deep at the base of the cerebrum. Strictly "nuclei" in the CNS, but the name stuck.

info.explanation: Group of deep telencephalic nuclei: caudate, putamen and globus pallidus (plus functionally related subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra).

facts.function: Selection and initiation of voluntary movement; also habits, reward and cognition.
facts.supply: Lenticulostriate arteries (from MCA), anterior choroidal artery.
facts.lesion: Parkinson disease (loss of nigrostriatal dopamine), Huntington disease (caudate degeneration), hemiballismus (subthalamic infarct).
facts.connections: Cortex - striatum - pallidum - thalamus - cortex loops.

etymology.story: The structure's curled shape reminded the Venetian anatomist Aranzi in 1564 of a seahorse (Greek hippokampos, horse + sea monster); it is also supposed to resemble a ram's horn, hence "cornu Ammonis".

info.explanation: Curved cortical structure on the medial temporal lobe floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.

facts.function: Forms new declarative (episodic) memories and spatial navigation.
facts.supply: Posterior cerebral artery (and anterior choroidal artery).
facts.lesion: Bilateral damage causes anterograde amnesia (HM; Alzheimer disease starts here); also a seizure focus in mesial temporal sclerosis.
facts.connections: Input from entorhinal cortex; output via the fornix to the mammillary bodies.

etymology.story: From Greek amygdale, "almond", also the root of amygdalin; the nucleus is almond-shaped.

info.explanation: Almond-shaped nuclear complex in the anterior medial temporal lobe, just anterior to the hippocampus.

facts.function: Processing of emotions, especially fear, and emotional memory; links sensation with autonomic and hormonal responses.
facts.supply: Anterior choroidal and middle cerebral artery branches.
facts.lesion: Kluver-Bucy syndrome (bilateral lesion): placidity, hypersexuality, hyperorality.
facts.connections: Connected to hypothalamus via the stria terminalis and ventral amygdalofugal pathway.

etymology.story: Gyrus is Latinised Greek gyros, "circle, ring", a convolution of the cortex.

info.explanation: Cortical gyrus on the medial temporal lobe, adjacent to the hippocampus and including the entorhinal cortex.

facts.function: Contextual memory and scene processing; entorhinal cortex relays into the hippocampus.
facts.lesion: Medial temporal atrophy in Alzheimer disease; seizures from mesial temporal sclerosis.
facts.connections: Entorhinal cortex gives the perforant path to the hippocampus.

etymology.story: Latin uncus is a hook (hence "uncinate").

info.explanation: Hook-shaped medial protrusion of the anterior parahippocampal gyrus.

facts.function: Contains primary olfactory cortex (piriform area).
facts.lesion: Uncal herniation through the tentorial notch compresses CN III (blown pupil) and the cerebral peduncle.

etymology.story: Greek thalamos meant the inner room of a house, the bedchamber; Galen used it for the deep brain region where the optic nerves seemed to arise.

info.explanation: Paired egg-shaped diencephalic masses on either side of the third ventricle.

facts.function: Relay and gatekeeper for all sensory information (except olfaction) to the cortex; also motor, limbic and arousal functions.
facts.supply: Thalamogeniculate and thalamoperforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery.
facts.lesion: Thalamic infarct causes contralateral sensory loss; Dejerine-Roussy thalamic pain syndrome; thalamic fatal familial insomnia.
facts.connections: Reciprocal connections with the cortex; receives ascending sensory pathways.

etymology.story: Literally the structure below the thalamus.

info.explanation: Small diencephalic region below the thalamus and around the third ventricle, with the mammillary bodies, tuber cinereum and infundibulum.

facts.function: Homeostasis: temperature, thirst, hunger, circadian rhythm, autonomic control and the pituitary.
facts.supply: Anterior and posterior communicating artery branches.
facts.lesion: Lesions cause diabetes insipidus, hyperthermia/hypothermia, obesity or anorexia, sleep disorders.
facts.connections: Connects with the pituitary, limbic system and brainstem autonomic centres.

etymology.story: Also called the massa intermedia; it is not a true commissure with decussating axons.

info.explanation: Band of grey matter bridging the two thalami across the third ventricle.

facts.function: Not a true commissure; it has no clear function and is absent in some people.

etymology.story: Chi, the Greek letter X; the same word underlies "chiasmus" in rhetoric.

info.explanation: X-shaped junction of the optic nerves where nasal retinal fibres cross to the opposite optic tract.

facts.function: Partial decussation allowing each hemisphere to receive the contralateral visual field.
facts.passes: Nasal retinal fibres decussate; temporal fibres remain ipsilateral.
facts.supply: Superior hypophyseal artery and circle of Willis branches.
facts.lesion: Pituitary adenoma compresses the crossing fibres causing bitemporal hemianopia.
facts.connections: Optic nerves to optic tracts.

etymology.story: Mamilla is the diminutive of mamma "breast": the two rounded bulges on the hypothalamic floor look like breasts.

info.explanation: Paired round bulges on the ventral surface of the hypothalamus, behind the tuber cinereum.

facts.function: Memory circuit (Papez circuit): receive fornix, project to the anterior thalamic nucleus.
facts.supply: Posterior communicating and posterior cerebral artery branches.
facts.lesion: Damage (thiamine deficiency, Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) causes anterograde amnesia and confabulation.
facts.connections: Fornix -> mammillary bodies -> mammillothalamic tract -> anterior thalamic nucleus.

lists.note: Pituitary Stalk (usually ripped, know general location)

etymology.story: Infundibulum literally means a funnel: it connects the hypothalamus to the pituitary like a funnel to a vessel.

info.explanation: Thin stalk linking the hypothalamus with the pituitary gland (hypophysis).

facts.function: Carries hypophysial portal vessels and hypothalamo-neurohypophysial axons.
facts.passes: Hypothalamic neurosecretory axons and portal vessels.
facts.lesion: Stalk transection or compression can cause diabetes insipidus and hyperprolactinaemia.

etymology.story: Mesencephalon is Greek for "middle brain", the most rostral part of the brainstem.

info.explanation: Rostral brainstem segment containing the tectum, tegmentum and cerebral peduncles.

facts.function: Visual and auditory reflexes, oculomotor control and motor and arousal systems.
facts.passes: Descending corticospinal fibres in the peduncle; ascending medial lemniscus.
facts.supply: Posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries and basilar tip penetrators.
facts.lesion: Weber syndrome: ipsilateral CN III palsy plus contralateral hemiparesis.
facts.connections: Contains CN III and IV nuclei.

etymology.story: Named by Varolius in the 16th century because it looks like a bridge arching between the cerebellar hemispheres.

info.explanation: Brainstem segment between midbrain and medulla, with a ventral basis pontis and dorsal tegmentum.

facts.function: Relays cortical information to the cerebellum via the pontine nuclei; houses nuclei of CN V-VIII and respiratory centres.
facts.passes: Corticospinal and corticopontine fibres in the basis.
facts.supply: Pontine arteries from the basilar artery.
facts.lesion: Locked-in syndrome after basilar artery occlusion; pontine haemorrhage causes pinpoint pupils and coma.
facts.connections: Middle cerebellar peduncle.

etymology.story: Medulla meant "marrow" or "pith", as in bone marrow; the medulla oblongata is the "oblong marrow".

info.explanation: Caudal brainstem segment continuous with the spinal cord, containing the pyramids and olives.

facts.function: Control of breathing, blood pressure, swallowing and vomiting; houses nuclei of CN IX-XII.
facts.supply: Vertebral arteries, anterior spinal and PICA branches.
facts.lesion: Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal artery) and lateral (Wallenberg, PICA/vertebral).
facts.connections: Gracile and cuneate nuclei and olive.

etymology.story: Motor is Latin for "mover", from movere. Brodmann area 4 is the cortex whose stimulation by Penfield produced movements in the body map.

info.explanation: Cortex of the precentral gyrus (Brodmann area 4), with giant Betz cells in layer V, laid out as the motor homunculus.

facts.function: Initiates voluntary movement of the contralateral body via the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts.
facts.passes: Corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts descend via the internal capsule.
facts.supply: Anterior cerebral artery (leg), middle cerebral artery (arm, face).
facts.lesion: Contralateral weakness (UMN signs); ACA infarct spares the face and arm but paralyses the leg.
facts.connections: Receives from premotor cortex, S1 and thalamus (VL).

etymology.story: Homunculus, a diminutive of homo, "man", the same word alchemists used for a tiny artificial human.

info.explanation: Map of the contralateral body across the precentral gyrus: legs on the medial surface, trunk and arm on the convexity, face and tongue laterally.

facts.function: Shows body areas disproportionately: hands, face and tongue are enormous because they need fine motor control.
facts.supply: ACA supplies leg area; MCA supplies arm and face area.

etymology.story: It lies anterior to primary motor cortex (BA 6) and prepares movements; prae means "before".

info.explanation: Brodmann area 6 anterior to the precentral gyrus, including the premotor cortex laterally and the supplementary motor area medially.

facts.function: Planning and sequencing of movement, guided by external cues (premotor) or internal cues (SMA).
facts.supply: Middle cerebral artery (lateral), anterior cerebral artery (SMA medial).
facts.lesion: Apraxia; SMA lesions cause transient akinesia and mutism.
facts.connections: Projects to M1 and the corticospinal tract.

roots.meaning: surname of Paul Broca (1824-1880), the surgeon and anthropologist who described the area

etymology.story: An eponym: Broca examined the patient "Tan" in 1861, who could say only that syllable, and found a lesion in the left inferior frontal gyrus. The Latin name area Broca simply attaches his name to the cortical region.

info.explanation: Left inferior frontal gyrus, pars opercularis and triangularis (Brodmann areas 44 and 45).

facts.function: Production of speech (motor programming of language) and grammar.
facts.passes: Arcuate fasciculus connects it to Wernicke's area.
facts.supply: Superior division of the middle cerebral artery.
facts.lesion: Broca (non-fluent, expressive) aphasia: halting effortful speech with good comprehension and poor repetition.
facts.connections: Connected to Wernicke's area via the arcuate fasciculus.

etymology.story: Cingulum is Latin for belt, from cingere "to gird"; the gyrus wraps the corpus callosum like a belt.

info.explanation: Anterior part of the cingulate gyrus (Brodmann areas 24, 32, 33) curved around the genu of the corpus callosum.

facts.function: Emotion, error monitoring, pain affect, motivation and autonomic control.
facts.supply: Pericallosal and callosomarginal branches of the anterior cerebral artery.
facts.lesion: Akinetic mutism and apathy after bilateral ACA infarcts; abulia.
facts.connections: Connections to prefrontal cortex, amygdala and thalamus.

etymology.story: Prefrontal means "in front of the frontal motor areas".

info.explanation: Lateral prefrontal cortex on the middle and superior frontal gyri (Brodmann areas 9 and 46).

facts.function: Executive function: working memory, planning, attention and cognitive flexibility.
facts.lesion: Dysexecutive syndrome: poor planning, perseveration and abulia; frontal-lobe disinhibition.
facts.connections: Reciprocal connections with the caudate and thalamus (mediodorsal nucleus).

etymology.story: The orbit, from orbis "circle, wheel", is the round eye socket; this cortex lies on the inferior frontal surface above it.

info.explanation: Prefrontal cortex on the ventral frontal surface above the orbits (Brodmann areas 11 and 47).

facts.function: Value-based decisions, reward, social behaviour and inhibition; secondary olfactory cortex.
facts.supply: Anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery branches.
facts.lesion: Disinhibition and socially inappropriate behaviour, as in Phineas Gage.
facts.connections: Connected to the amygdala and dorsomedial thalamus.

etymology.story: Ventral (belly side) and medial prefrontal cortex.

info.explanation: Medial and inferior prefrontal cortex (Brodmann areas 10, 11, 25 and 32).

facts.function: Emotion regulation, value-based decision-making and social cognition.
facts.lesion: Poor decisions and emotional blunting despite intact IQ.
facts.connections: Strong amygdala and hypothalamic connections.

etymology.story: Named for the many small holes made by the lenticulostriate and other penetrating arteries entering the brain.

info.explanation: Region at the base of the brain between the optic tract and olfactory trigone where small vessels perforate to supply deep structures.

facts.function: Entry point for the medial and lateral striate arteries.
facts.supply: Lenticulostriate arteries (from the MCA) and medial striate arteries.
facts.lesion: Lacunar infarcts in deep structures.

etymology.story: Soma is Greek for body; "somatic" means "of the body".

info.explanation: Postcentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 3, 1 and 2) receiving touch, vibration and proprioception from the contralateral body.

facts.function: Conscious perception and localisation of touch, vibration, pain and proprioception.
facts.passes: Thalamocortical projection passes through the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
facts.supply: Anterior cerebral artery (leg) and middle cerebral artery (arm, face).
facts.lesion: Contralateral sensory loss, astereognosis and loss of two-point discrimination.
facts.connections: Receives from VPL/VPM thalamus.

etymology.story: Penfield and Rasmussen drew the map of the body surface on the postcentral gyrus.

info.explanation: Map of the contralateral body across the postcentral gyrus with the legs medial, hands and face lateral.

facts.function: Shows disproportionate representation of the lips, tongue and hands.

etymology.story: Associare = ad + sociare, "to join together", the root of "association".

info.explanation: Posterior parietal cortex (Brodmann areas 5 and 7) integrating tactile and proprioceptive information with vision.

facts.function: Stereognosis, body schema and visuospatial integration.
facts.lesion: Astereognosis, tactile agnosia and hemispatial neglect (right side).
facts.connections: Receives from S1.

lists.note: Multimodal area (Parietal lobe general association area)

etymology.literal: joining area of the wall bone
etymology.story: Parietal comes from the parietal bone; paries is Latin for wall.

info.explanation: Posterior parietal cortex integrating sensory modalities for spatial attention and awareness.

facts.function: Spatial attention and awareness of the body and its surroundings; praxis in the dominant hemisphere.
facts.lesion: Right parietal lesion: contralateral hemineglect; left lesion: Gerstmann syndrome.

etymology.story: Visus is the Latin word for sight; Brodmann area 17, also called striate cortex because of the stripe of Gennari.

info.explanation: Occipital cortex on the banks of the calcarine fissure (Brodmann area 17).

facts.function: Conscious perception of the contralateral visual field.
facts.supply: Calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery; MCA supplies the macular tip.
facts.lesion: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing in PCA stroke.
facts.connections: Receives from the lateral geniculate nucleus.

etymology.story: Association cortex builds meaning from basic visual features.

info.explanation: Brodmann areas 18 and 19 around V1, with dorsal (where) and ventral (what) streams.

facts.function: Processing of form, colour, motion and object recognition.
facts.lesion: Visual agnosia; prosopagnosia (fusiform face area); Balint syndrome.
facts.connections: Receives from V1.

etymology.story: Audire, "to hear", gives "audio" and "audience".

info.explanation: Transverse temporal gyri of Heschl (Brodmann areas 41 and 42) in the superior temporal plane.

facts.function: Conscious perception of sound; tonotopic map.
facts.passes: Auditory radiation from the MGN passes through the sublenticular limb of the internal capsule.
facts.lesion: Unilateral lesion causes little deficit because of bilateral input; bilateral causes cortical deafness.
facts.connections: Receives from the medial geniculate nucleus.

etymology.story: Joins raw sounds to meaning.

info.explanation: Superior temporal gyrus around A1 (Brodmann area 22) analysing complex sounds.

facts.function: Interpretation of sounds, speech and music.
facts.lesion: Auditory agnosia; amusia.
facts.connections: Receives from A1.

roots.meaning: surname of Carl Wernicke (1848-1905), the neurologist who described it

etymology.story: An eponym: in 1874 Wernicke described patients who spoke fluently but could not understand language, and linked this to damage in the posterior left superior temporal gyrus.

info.explanation: Posterior part of the left superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann area 22, sometimes with 39 and 40).

facts.function: Comprehension of spoken and written language.
facts.passes: Arcuate fasciculus connects it to Broca's area.
facts.supply: Inferior division of the middle cerebral artery.
facts.lesion: Wernicke (fluent, receptive) aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension.
facts.connections: Connects to Broca's area via arcuate fasciculus.

etymology.story: The temple is the region where hair first greys, the passage of time.

info.explanation: Temporal association cortex (Brodmann 20, 21, 37, 38) for object identification, memory and language.

facts.function: Object and face recognition, semantic memory and language.
facts.lesion: Agnosia, anomia; semantic dementia.

etymology.story: Fibres associating cortical areas within one hemisphere.

info.explanation: White matter tracts linking cortical regions within the same hemisphere (e.g. arcuate and uncinate fasciculi, cingulum).

facts.function: Integrate different cortical areas in one hemisphere.
facts.lesion: Arcuate fasciculus lesion causes conduction aphasia.

etymology.story: Commissure comes from committere, "to bring together".

info.explanation: Fibres crossing the midline to connect the two hemispheres (corpus callosum, anterior and posterior commissures).

facts.function: Interhemispheric transfer of information.
facts.lesion: Callosal disconnection.

etymology.story: Projection fibres "project" from the cortex to subcortical targets and the other way.

info.explanation: Fibres linking the cortex with the thalamus, brainstem and spinal cord, passing through the internal capsule and corona radiata.

facts.function: Carry cortical output and thalamocortical input.
facts.passes: Internal capsule, corona radiata, corticospinal tract.
facts.lesion: Capsular stroke causes contralateral hemiplegia.

etymology.story: Small white matter bundle crossing in the lamina terminalis.

info.explanation: Small commissure crossing the midline in the lamina terminalis, connecting the temporal lobes, amygdalae and olfactory structures.

facts.function: Interhemispheric transfer between temporal lobes and olfactory bulbs.
facts.passes: Fibres between the two temporal lobes (amygdala) and olfactory tracts.

etymology.story: Capsula is a diminutive of capsa, "box", so the capsule is a little box-like band of white matter enclosing the lentiform nucleus.

info.explanation: V-shaped white matter band between the caudate and thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally, with an anterior limb, genu and posterior limb.

facts.function: Funnels all corticofugal and thalamocortical projection fibres.
facts.passes: Corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts (genu and posterior limb), thalamocortical and corticopontine fibres.
facts.supply: Lenticulostriate (MCA), anterior choroidal and ACA (Heubner) arteries.
facts.lesion: Lacunar stroke causes pure motor hemiparesis.

lists.note: Interhemispheric Fissure or Median Longitudinal Cerebral Fissure
Median Longitudinal Cerebral Fissure or the Interhemispheric Fissure

etymology.story: Hemi is "half" and sphaira "ball".

info.explanation: Deep midline cleft separating the two cerebral hemispheres; the falx cerebri lies in it.

facts.function: Separates the hemispheres.
facts.supply: Anterior cerebral arteries run in it.

etymology.story: Also the Sylvian fissure, for Franciscus Sylvius, a 17th century Dutch physician.

info.explanation: Deep groove separating the frontal and parietal lobes from the temporal lobe, containing the insula and middle cerebral artery.

facts.function: Landmark: contains the insular cortex and MCA branches.
facts.supply: Middle cerebral artery runs in it.
facts.lesion: MCA aneurysms located here.

info.review_note: Sylvius attribution: Franciscus vs Jacobus Sylvius is debated.

etymology.story: Sulcus means a furrow, as in plough furrow; the central sulcus (Rolando) lies midway along the hemisphere.

info.explanation: Groove separating the frontal lobe (precentral gyrus) from the parietal lobe (postcentral gyrus).

facts.function: Landmark dividing motor and sensory cortex.

etymology.story: Boundary between parietal and occipital lobes on the medial surface.

info.explanation: Medial cleft between the parietal and occipital lobes, meeting the calcarine fissure.

facts.function: Landmark dividing parietal and occipital lobes.

etymology.story: Divides the posterior parietal cortex into superior and inferior lobules.

info.explanation: Horizontal groove dividing the superior and inferior parietal lobules.

facts.function: Landmark; houses areas for visuomotor and spatial attention.

etymology.story: From calcar, a spur (as in "calcaneus"), since it forms a spur-like bulge in the occipital horn (calcar avis, "bird's spur").

info.explanation: Medial occipital groove with the primary visual cortex on its banks.

facts.function: Landmark for V1: the cuneus above it receives the lower visual field and the lingual gyrus below it the upper field.
facts.lesion: Occipital stroke causes homonymous hemianopia.

info.review_note: Check which bank (cuneus vs lingual) gets which field with the lab slides.

etymology.story: Gyrus from Greek gyros "ring"; a gyrus is a ridge between sulci.

info.explanation: Uppermost gyrus on the lateral frontal lobe, continuing medially to the supplementary motor area.

facts.function: Executive and motor planning; self-awareness.

etymology.story: Middle gyrus of the three frontal gyri.

info.explanation: Lateral frontal gyrus containing the frontal eye field and DLPFC.

facts.function: Working memory, gaze (frontal eye field).
facts.lesion: Contralateral gaze palsy: eyes deviate toward lesion.

etymology.story: Contains the opercular and triangular parts forming Broca's area on the left.

info.explanation: Gyrus with pars opercularis, triangularis and orbitalis.

facts.function: Speech production on the left (Broca).
facts.lesion: Broca aphasia.

etymology.story: Wraps around the corpus callosum like a belt.

info.explanation: Medial gyrus above the corpus callosum, part of the limbic system.

facts.function: Emotion, pain, attention.
facts.lesion: Subfalcine herniation compresses it.
facts.connections: Connected to the hippocampus via the cingulum.

etymology.story: Lies anterior to the central sulcus.

info.explanation: Frontal gyrus just anterior to the central sulcus containing the primary motor cortex (BA 4).

facts.function: Voluntary motor control of the contralateral body.
facts.lesion: Contralateral paralysis.

etymology.story: Lies posterior to the central sulcus.

info.explanation: Parietal gyrus just posterior to the central sulcus containing S1 (BA 3, 1, 2).

facts.function: Conscious somatic sensation.
facts.lesion: Contralateral sensory loss.

etymology.story: Lobule is a diminutive of lobus, "lobe".

info.explanation: Parietal lobule above the intraparietal sulcus (BA 5 and 7).

facts.function: Spatial orientation and somatosensory integration.
facts.lesion: Astereognosis; optic ataxia.

etymology.story: Contains the supramarginal and angular gyri (BA 40 and 39).

info.explanation: Parietal lobule below the intraparietal sulcus containing supramarginal (BA 40) and angular (BA 39) gyri.

facts.function: Language, calculation, spatial attention.
facts.supply: Inferior division of the middle cerebral artery.
facts.lesion: Gerstmann syndrome (left); contralateral neglect (right).

etymology.story: Houses primary auditory cortex and Wernicke's area.

info.explanation: Uppermost temporal gyrus below the lateral fissure containing auditory areas and Wernicke's area.

facts.function: Hearing and language comprehension.
facts.supply: Inferior division of the middle cerebral artery.
facts.lesion: Wernicke aphasia.

etymology.story: The middle of three temporal gyri.

info.explanation: Lateral temporal gyrus involved in semantic memory and motion perception (MT/V5).

facts.function: Semantic processing and motion perception.

etymology.story: Part of the ventral visual (what) stream.

info.explanation: Gyrus on the inferior lateral temporal lobe involved in object and face recognition.

facts.function: Visual object and face recognition.
facts.supply: Posterior cerebral and middle cerebral arteries.
facts.lesion: Visual agnosia, prosopagnosia.

etymology.story: Described by Richard Heschl in 1878, so also "Heschl's gyrus".

info.explanation: Gyrus lying across the superior temporal plane containing the primary auditory cortex.

facts.function: Primary auditory cortex (BA 41, 42).
facts.supply: Inferior division of the middle cerebral artery.
facts.connections: Receives from medial geniculate nucleus.

etymology.story: Vertebra comes from vertere, "to turn": the bones through which the spine turns and twists.

info.explanation: Weight-bearing anterior cylinder of a vertebra, increasing in size from cervical to lumbar.

facts.function: Supports body weight; separated from its neighbours by intervertebral discs.
facts.lesion: Compression fractures in osteoporosis; metastasis to the body can compress the cord.

etymology.story: Foramen is Latin for hole or opening, from forare, "to bore".

info.explanation: Opening bounded by the body and arch; stacked, they form the vertebral canal.

facts.function: Encloses the spinal cord and meninges.
facts.lesion: Stenosis narrows it and compresses the cord or roots.

etymology.story: Arcus is a bow or arch, as in "archery".

info.explanation: Posterior part of the vertebra, formed by pedicles and laminae, enclosing the vertebral foramen.

facts.function: Protects the spinal cord.
facts.lesion: Laminectomy removes it to decompress the cord.

etymology.story: Transverse processes project laterally to the sides, "across" the axis of the spine.

info.explanation: Lateral projection from the junction of pedicle and lamina on each side.

facts.function: Muscle and ligament attachment; articulates with ribs in the thoracic spine.

etymology.story: Spina is Latin for thorn; spine also names the whole vertebral column because of the row of thorn-like processes.

info.explanation: Posterior midline projection of the vertebral arch, palpable under the skin.

facts.function: Muscle and ligament attachment; palpable landmark for lumbar puncture.

etymology.story: Discus is the Greek quoit thrown by athletes, referring to the flat round shape.

info.explanation: Fibrocartilaginous cushion with an outer annulus fibrosus and central nucleus pulposus between vertebral bodies.

facts.function: Shock absorption and flexibility of the spine.
facts.lesion: Herniation (typically posterolateral) compresses the nerve root exiting at that level or below (e.g. L5/S1 compresses S1).

etymology.story: The gap between adjacent vertebral pedicles.

info.explanation: Opening between adjacent vertebrae bounded by the pedicles, vertebral bodies and facet joints.

facts.function: Passage for the spinal nerve and radicular vessels.
facts.lesion: Foraminal stenosis or disc herniation compresses the nerve root.

etymology.story: Canalis, a pipe or channel, from canna "reed"; the same root as "canal" and "channel".

info.explanation: Continuous tube formed by the stacked vertebral foramina, containing the spinal cord and meninges.

facts.function: Houses and protects the spinal cord, meninges, epidural space and roots.
facts.passes: Spinal cord, cauda equina, epidural fat and venous plexus.
facts.lesion: Spinal stenosis and epidural abscess compress the contents.

lists.note: Distinguish cervical, thoracic, lumbar and sacral vertebrae

etymology.story: Cervix is the neck; it also names the neck of the uterus.

info.explanation: Seven vertebrae (C1-C7) of the neck, with transverse foramina for the vertebral arteries.

facts.function: Support and move the head; protect the cervical cord.
facts.passes: Vertebral arteries pass through transverse foramina C1-C6.
facts.lesion: Fracture or dislocation can cause quadriplegia; C3-C5 injuries affect phrenic nerve and respiration.

lists.note: Distinguish cervical, thoracic, lumbar and sacral vertebrae

etymology.story: Thorax is the Greek word for chest and also for a breastplate or cuirass.

info.explanation: Twelve vertebrae (T1-T12) with facets for rib articulation.

facts.function: Support the rib cage.

lists.note: Distinguish cervical, thoracic, lumbar and sacral vertebrae

etymology.story: Lumbus is Latin for loin, giving "lumbar" and "lumbago".

info.explanation: Five large vertebrae (L1-L5) of the lower back with no costal facets.

facts.function: Bear most of the body weight.
facts.lesion: Disc herniation; lumbar puncture below L2 to avoid the cord.

lists.note: Distinguish cervical, thoracic, lumbar and sacral vertebrae

etymology.story: Sacrum means "sacred", from the Latin os sacrum; it was thought either to be offered in sacrifice or the seat of the soul.

info.explanation: Five fused vertebrae (S1-S5) forming the triangular sacrum.

facts.function: Connects the spine to the pelvis.
facts.lesion: Sacral fracture can injure the sacral roots (bladder, bowel and sexual function).

info.review_note: Sacrum "sacred bone" explanation (sacrificial offering) is traditional, not certain.

etymology.story: Conus is Latin for cone, from Greek konos; the tapered end of the spinal cord.

info.explanation: Tapered caudal end of the spinal cord, ending at about the L1-L2 vertebral level in adults.

facts.function: Contains the sacral and coccygeal segments.
facts.supply: Anterior spinal artery and artery of Adamkiewicz.
facts.lesion: Conus medullaris syndrome gives early bladder/bowel dysfunction and saddle anaesthesia.

etymology.story: Anatomists thought the bundle of lumbar and sacral roots resembled a horse's tail.

info.explanation: Bundle of lumbar and sacral spinal nerve roots descending in the lumbar cistern below the conus medullaris.

facts.function: Carries lower limb, bladder and bowel roots.
facts.lesion: Cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency: saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention and leg weakness.

etymology.story: A thread that terminates the spinal cord (filum is the same root as "filament").

info.explanation: Thin pial thread descending from the conus to the coccyx, anchoring the cord.

facts.function: Anchors the cord to the coccyx.
facts.lesion: Tethered cord syndrome.

etymology.story: Denticulus is a diminutive of dens, "tooth": the ligament's edge has tooth-like points where it attaches to the dura.

info.explanation: Lateral extensions of the pia mater between dorsal and ventral roots, attaching to the dura at 21 points.

facts.function: Suspend the spinal cord in the middle of the dural sac.
facts.lesion: Landmark for cordotomy; reduces cord movement.

lists.note: Dorsal and Ventral Rootlets and Roots

etymology.story: Radix is root and radicula a little root.

info.explanation: Fine bundles of sensory axons emerging from the dorsolateral sulcus of the cord that merge into the dorsal root.

facts.function: Carry afferent axons into the cord.

lists.note: Dorsal and Ventral Rootlets and Roots

etymology.story: Little roots from the ventral (anterior) side.

info.explanation: Fine bundles of motor axons emerging from the ventrolateral sulcus that merge into the ventral root.

facts.function: Carry efferent axons out of the cord.
facts.passes: Alpha, gamma motor neuron axons and preganglionic autonomic axons.

lists.note: Dorsal and Ventral Rootlets and Roots

etymology.story: Radix gave us "radish", "radical" and "eradicate".

info.explanation: Root of a spinal nerve formed by the dorsal rootlets, carrying sensory fibres to the DRG.

facts.function: Carries somatic and visceral sensory axons into the cord.
facts.lesion: Compression causes radicular pain in a dermatomal distribution.
facts.connections: Cell bodies in the DRG.

lists.note: Dorsal and Ventral Rootlets and Roots

etymology.story: Ventral root carries efferent fibres out of the cord (Bell-Magendie law).

info.explanation: Root formed by the ventral rootlets, carrying motor axons.

facts.function: Carries motor and (T1-L2, S2-S4) autonomic efferents out of the cord.
facts.lesion: Compression causes myotomal weakness.
facts.connections: Cell bodies in ventral horn (and lateral horn).

etymology.story: Ganglion originally meant a swelling or knot under the skin.

info.explanation: Swelling on the dorsal root containing the cell bodies of primary sensory neurons.

facts.function: Houses the cell bodies of first-order sensory neurons (pseudounipolar).
facts.lesion: Herpes zoster reactivates in the DRG (dermatomal rash); the ganglion lacks a blood-nerve barrier.
facts.connections: First-order neuron bodies; pseudounipolar neurons.

etymology.story: The dura continues around each root as a sleeve and fuses with the epineurium at the intervertebral foramen.

info.explanation: Dural extensions around the spinal roots as they exit through the intervertebral foramina, continuous with the epineurium.

facts.function: Protect the roots.

etymology.story: Nervus meant sinew or tendon; only later did "nerve" come to mean the conduction cords.

info.explanation: 31 pairs of mixed nerves formed by the union of dorsal and ventral roots: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal.

facts.function: Carry both sensory and motor signals between the cord and the body.
facts.lesion: Radiculopathy: dermatomal pain, myotomal weakness, reflex loss.

etymology.story: Ramus is a branch; dorsal ramus supplies the back.

info.explanation: Branch of the spinal nerve supplying the deep back muscles and overlying skin.

facts.function: Innervates intrinsic back muscles and paraspinal skin.

etymology.story: The ventral ramus supplies the anterolateral trunk and limbs and forms the plexuses.

info.explanation: Larger branch of the spinal nerve supplying the anterior and lateral body wall and the limbs; forms the plexuses.

facts.function: Innervates limbs and ventrolateral trunk.

etymology.story: Brachium, "arm", from Greek brachion; plexus is something plaited or woven.

info.explanation: Network formed by ventral rami of C5-T1 supplying the upper limb, organised roots - trunks - divisions - cords - branches.

facts.function: Innervates the upper limb muscles and skin.
facts.passes: Roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches (e.g., axillary, musculocutaneous, median, radial, ulnar).
facts.lesion: Erb palsy (C5-C6, waiter's tip); Klumpke palsy (C8-T1, claw hand).

etymology.story: Plaited network of lower limb nerves.

info.explanation: Network formed by ventral rami of L1-S4 supplying the lower limb (lumbar plexus L1-L4 and sacral plexus L4-S4).

facts.function: Innervates the lower limb, including femoral, obturator and sciatic nerves.
facts.passes: Femoral, obturator, sciatic (tibial, common fibular) and pudendal nerves.
facts.lesion: Sciatica from L4-S3 root compression; femoral neuropathy.

etymology.story: In cross-section the grey matter looks like a butterfly with horns.

info.explanation: Posterior part of the spinal grey matter that receives somatic sensory input from the dorsal roots (laminae I-VI).

facts.function: Processes and relays pain, temperature and touch to ascending tracts.
facts.lesion: Spinal lesions cause segmental loss of pain and temperature sensation.
facts.connections: Receives primary afferents; projects to anterolateral system.

etymology.story: Front horn of the butterfly-shaped grey matter.

info.explanation: Anterior grey matter containing alpha and gamma lower motor neurons (lamina IX).

facts.function: Contains lower motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscle.
facts.lesion: Poliomyelitis, ALS: LMN signs (flaccid weakness, fasciculations, atrophy).
facts.connections: Receives corticospinal and other descending input.

etymology.story: Small lateral projection of the grey matter present only in T1-L2.

info.explanation: Intermediolateral cell column at T1-L2 containing sympathetic preganglionic neurons.

facts.function: Source of sympathetic outflow.
facts.lesion: Horner syndrome with T1 interruptions.
facts.connections: Preganglionic axons exit via the ventral root.

etymology.story: The grey matter between dorsal and ventral horns (lamina VII).

info.explanation: Spinal grey matter between dorsal and ventral horns, including Clarke's nucleus and the lateral horn; at S2-S4 it holds the sacral parasympathetic nucleus.

facts.function: Interneurons and autonomic preganglionic cells.

etymology.story: Columna means pillar, from celsus, "high"; these are the large white pillars at the back of the cord.

info.explanation: Ascending white matter in the dorsal funiculus composed of fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus.

facts.function: Carry fine touch, vibration, two-point discrimination and conscious proprioception ipsilaterally.
facts.passes: Fasciculus gracilis (lower body) and cuneatus (upper body); first-order axons.
facts.lesion: Lesion causes ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception below the level (positive Romberg); tabes dorsalis.
facts.connections: First-order axons from DRG ascend to the gracile and cuneate nuclei.

etymology.story: Gracilis means slender, thin; it is the narrow medial portion of the dorsal columns.

info.explanation: Medial part of the dorsal columns carrying sensation from the lower limb and lower trunk (below T6).

facts.function: Carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception from the legs.
facts.passes: First-order axons from sacral, lumbar and lower thoracic DRG.
facts.lesion: Ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception in the leg.
facts.connections: Terminates in the nucleus gracilis.

lists.group: Caudal Medulla – Level of Cuneate & Gracile Tubercles

etymology.story: Named for its wedge shape in cross-section.

info.explanation: Lateral part of the dorsal columns carrying sensation from the upper limb and upper trunk (above T6).

facts.function: Carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception from the arm.
facts.passes: First-order axons from cervical and upper thoracic DRG.
facts.lesion: Ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception in the arm.
facts.connections: Terminates in the nucleus cuneatus.

lists.group: Rostral Midbrain – Level of Superior Colliculus
Caudal Midbrain – Level of Inferior Colliculus
Rostral Pons – Level of Trigeminal Nerve
Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus
Caudal Medulla – Level of Cuneate & Gracile Tubercles

etymology.story: Named for its origin (spinal cord) and target (thalamus).

info.explanation: Ascending pathway of second-order neurons from the dorsal horn that cross in the ventral white commissure and ascend in the anterolateral white matter.

facts.function: Carries pain, temperature, itch and crude touch from the contralateral body.
facts.passes: Second-order neurons crossing in the ventral white commissure; spinothalamic fibres to VPL.
facts.lesion: Contralateral loss of pain and temperature starting about two segments below the lesion.
facts.connections: First-order Adelta and C fibres synapse in the dorsal horn; second-order axons cross within one or two segments.

lists.group: Caudal Medulla – Level of Cuneate & Gracile Tubercles

etymology.story: Named for its origin (spinal cord) and target (cerebellum).

info.explanation: Uncrossed tract from Clarke's nucleus (T1-L2) ascending in the dorsolateral funiculus and entering the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

facts.function: Carries unconscious proprioception from the lower limb to the ipsilateral cerebellum.
facts.passes: Second-order axons from Clarke's nucleus, ipsilateral, via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
facts.supply: Posterior spinal artery and anterior spinal artery branches.
facts.lesion: Ipsilateral limb ataxia; Friedreich ataxia.
facts.connections: First-order from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs, synapse in Clarke's nucleus.

etymology.literal: entry belt of the dorsal root
etymology.story: The region where the dorsal root enters the cord and its fibres sort by size.

info.explanation: Region where dorsal rootlets enter the cord, sorting afferent fibres into a medial division (large myelinated) and a lateral division (small fibres).

facts.function: Segregates large and small primary afferents.
facts.lesion: Syringomyelia and root avulsion affect it.

etymology.literal: lateral part of the root entry zone
etymology.story: Lateral fibres are small and carry pain and temperature.

info.explanation: Lateral division carrying small-diameter A-delta and C fibres that enter Lissauer's tract.

facts.function: Pain and temperature afferents.

etymology.literal: medial part of the root entry zone
etymology.story: Medial fibres are large and carry touch and proprioception.

info.explanation: Medial division carrying large-diameter A-alpha and A-beta fibres that enter the dorsal columns.

facts.function: Touch and proprioception afferents.

etymology.story: Marginal because it caps the dorsal horn tip (lamina I).

info.explanation: Lamina I at the tip of the dorsal horn.

facts.function: Relays pain and temperature to the anterolateral system.

etymology.story: Gelatina, "jelly", from gelare, "to freeze"; in unstained sections it appears gelatinous because it lacks myelin.

info.explanation: Lamina II of the dorsal horn, rich in small interneurons.

facts.function: Modulates pain transmission (gate control); opioid and enkephalin neurons.
facts.connections: Site of opioid action in the gate theory of pain.

etymology.story: Proprius means "one's own", so this nucleus is the dorsal horn's own principal nucleus (propriospinal also from this root).

info.explanation: Laminae III-IV of the dorsal horn.

facts.function: Processes touch and proprioceptive input and projects to the thalamus.

etymology.story: Named for the English anatomist Jacob Augustus Lockhart Clarke (1817-1880).

info.explanation: Nucleus dorsalis at the base of the dorsal horn, from T1 to L2/L3.

facts.function: Relay of lower limb unconscious proprioception to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
facts.passes: Source of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
facts.connections: Receives collaterals of group Ia/Ib afferents.

etymology.story: The place where spinothalamic axons cross, in front of the central canal.

info.explanation: White matter ventral to the central canal where second-order neurons of the anterolateral system decussate.

facts.function: Decussation site of the spinothalamic tract.
facts.passes: Crossing second-order axons of the spinothalamic tract.
facts.lesion: Syringomyelia: bilateral "cape-like" loss of pain and temperature, sparing touch.

lists.note: Anterior thalamic nuclei (creating anterior thalamic tubercles)
anterior thalamic nuclei (creating anterior thalamic tubercles)

etymology.story: Part of the Papez circuit for memory, named simply for its position at the front of the thalamus.

info.explanation: Nucleus at the anterior pole of the thalamus, receiving the mammillothalamic tract and projecting to the cingulate gyrus.

facts.function: Memory and learning (Papez circuit), limbic relay.
facts.lesion: Infarct causes anterograde amnesia; damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
facts.connections: Mammillary bodies -> anterior nucleus -> cingulate gyrus.

etymology.story: Pulvinus is a cushion or pillow, as in the pulvinar of a Roman temple where the gods' images were set; the posterior thalamus bulges like a cushion.

info.explanation: Large posterior nucleus of the thalamus forming a cushion over the midbrain.

facts.function: Visual attention and integration of visual, auditory and somatosensory information with association cortex.
facts.lesion: Contralateral visual neglect and attentional deficits.
facts.connections: Reciprocal connections with parietal, temporal and occipital association cortex and superior colliculus.

etymology.story: Geniculum is diminutive of genu, "knee": the nucleus is a small bent bump on the posterior thalamus like a bent knee.

info.explanation: Posterior thalamic nucleus that relays hearing from the inferior colliculus to the primary auditory cortex.

facts.function: Auditory relay nucleus.
facts.passes: Brachium of the inferior colliculus brings input; auditory radiation passes through the sublenticular internal capsule to A1.
facts.lesion: Contributes to deafness only when bilateral.
facts.connections: Inferior colliculus -> MGN -> primary auditory cortex.

etymology.story: Bent like a small knee, and located lateral to the MGN.

info.explanation: Six-layered posterior thalamic nucleus that relays vision from the optic tract to V1.

facts.function: Relay of visual information from the retina to the primary visual cortex.
facts.passes: Optic tract input; optic radiation output.
facts.supply: Anterior choroidal artery (lateral) and posterior cerebral artery.
facts.lesion: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
facts.connections: Retinal ganglion cells -> LGN -> optic radiations -> V1.

etymology.story: Epi- means "upon": the epithalamus lies on top of the thalamus and includes the habenula and pineal.

info.explanation: Dorsomedial diencephalon containing the habenular nuclei, stria medullaris and pineal gland.

facts.function: Links limbic forebrain with the midbrain; controls circadian rhythm via the pineal.
facts.passes: Stria medullaris, habenular and posterior commissures.
facts.lesion: Pineal tumours compress the tectum causing Parinaud syndrome.

etymology.story: Named for its resemblance to a pine cone; Descartes thought it the seat of the soul because it is a single midline structure.

info.explanation: Small midline endocrine gland at the posterior roof of the third ventricle.

facts.function: Secretes melatonin, regulating circadian rhythms.
facts.lesion: Calcifies with age (a midline marker on imaging); tumours cause Parinaud syndrome (impaired upgaze) and obstructive hydrocephalus.
facts.connections: Sympathetic input via the superior cervical ganglion, relayed from the suprachiasmatic nucleus.

etymology.story: From trahere, "to draw", as in "tractor"; the tract draws visual fibres from the chiasm to the LGN.

info.explanation: Pathway behind the optic chiasm carrying fibres from the ipsilateral temporal retina and the contralateral nasal retina to the LGN.

facts.function: Carries the contralateral visual field to the thalamus and midbrain.
facts.passes: Retinal ganglion cell axons from the ipsilateral temporal and contralateral nasal retina.
facts.lesion: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
facts.connections: Terminates in LGN, pretectum and superior colliculus.

lists.group: Rostral Midbrain – Level of Superior Colliculus

etymology.story: Old anatomists called the superior and inferior colliculi the nates and testes ("buttocks and testicles").

info.explanation: Layered structure on the dorsal midbrain tectum receiving direct retinal input.

facts.function: Controls visual reflexes, saccades and orienting head and eye movements; source of the tectospinal tract.
facts.lesion: Parinaud syndrome (impaired upgaze, light-near dissociation) with dorsal midbrain lesions.
facts.connections: Retina and visual cortex -> SC -> tectospinal tract.

lists.group: Caudal Midbrain – Level of Inferior Colliculus

etymology.story: The lower of the corpora quadrigemina.

info.explanation: Dorsal midbrain nucleus that is the obligate relay of ascending auditory information.

facts.function: Auditory processing and localisation of sound; auditory startle reflex.
facts.passes: Brachium of the inferior colliculus to the MGN; lateral lemniscus input.
facts.lesion: Bilateral lesions cause deafness.
facts.connections: Lateral lemniscus -> IC -> brachium -> MGN.

etymology.story: Brachium is Latin for arm (from Greek brachion).

info.explanation: Fibre bundle linking the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate nucleus.

facts.function: Carries auditory information to the thalamus.
facts.passes: Auditory fibres from IC to MGN.

lists.group: Rostral Midbrain – Level of Superior Colliculus
Caudal Midbrain – Level of Inferior Colliculus

etymology.story: Pedunculus is a diminutive of pes, "foot"; the same word as a flower stalk, "peduncle".

info.explanation: Pair of ventral midbrain columns (crus cerebri plus tegmentum) emerging from the pons.

facts.function: Conduct cortical descending fibres to the pons and spinal cord.
facts.passes: Corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine fibres in the crus cerebri.
facts.supply: Posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries.
facts.lesion: Weber syndrome: ipsilateral CN III palsy plus contralateral hemiparesis.

lists.group: Rostral Midbrain – Level of Superior Colliculus

etymology.story: A fossa is a ditch; this one is between the two peduncles.

info.explanation: Midline depression on the ventral midbrain between the cerebral peduncles, containing the posterior perforated substance.

facts.function: Exit point of the oculomotor nerve.
facts.supply: Basilar tip and posterior communicating artery penetrators.
facts.lesion: Oculomotor palsy from posterior communicating aneurysm or herniation.

etymology.story: Three paired stalks anchor the cerebellum to the brainstem.

info.explanation: Three paired stalks (superior, middle, inferior) carrying all cerebellar input and output.

facts.function: Connect the cerebellum with the midbrain, pons and medulla.

lists.group: Rostral Pons – Level of Trigeminal Nerve
Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus

etymology.story: Connects the cerebellum with the midbrain.

info.explanation: Main efferent pathway from the cerebellum (dentate to red nucleus and thalamus) plus the ventral spinocerebellar tract input.

facts.function: Carries most cerebellar output.
facts.lesion: Ipsilateral limb ataxia and tremor.
facts.connections: Decussates in the midbrain.

lists.group: Rostral Pons – Level of Trigeminal Nerve
Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus

etymology.story: The largest stalk, the one lying in the pons.

info.explanation: Largest peduncle, carrying contralateral pontocerebellar fibres from the pontine nuclei.

facts.function: Carries cortical information via the pons to the cerebellum.
facts.connections: Entirely afferent.

etymology.story: Connects the medulla with the cerebellum; the restiform body.

info.explanation: Carries mostly afferent fibres: dorsal spinocerebellar, cuneocerebellar and olivocerebellar fibres, plus vestibulocerebellar fibres.

facts.function: Carries proprioceptive, vestibular and olivary input to the cerebellum.
facts.passes: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract, climbing fibres from the olive.
facts.lesion: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome ipsilateral ataxia.

lists.group: Rostral Pons – Level of Trigeminal Nerve
Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus
