Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus
Caudal Medulla – Level of Cuneate & Gracile Tubercles

etymology.story: Lemniscus is the Greek word for a ribbon or woolen fillet worn on the head.

info.explanation: Ribbon-like ascending bundle of second-order DCML axons from the gracile and cuneate nuclei to the contralateral VPL thalamus.

facts.function: Carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception.
facts.passes: Second-order axons that cross as the internal arcuate fibres.
facts.supply: Anterior spinal (medulla), basilar paramedian and posterior cerebral (midbrain) arteries.
facts.lesion: Lesion causes contralateral loss of vibration and proprioception.
facts.connections: Gracile and cuneate nuclei -> medial lemniscus -> VPL.

lists.group: Rostral Midbrain – Level of Superior Colliculus
Caudal Midbrain – Level of Inferior Colliculus
Rostral Pons – Level of Trigeminal Nerve
Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus

etymology.story: A longitudinal bundle running near the midline of the brainstem.

info.explanation: Paired bundle near the midline connecting the vestibular nuclei and the nuclei of CN III, IV and VI.

facts.function: Coordinates conjugate horizontal eye movements and vestibulo-ocular reflexes.
facts.lesion: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (adduction failure on the side of lesion with abducting nystagmus), typical in multiple sclerosis.
facts.connections: Links abducens nucleus to contralateral oculomotor nucleus.

lists.group: Caudal Midbrain – Level of Inferior Colliculus
Caudal Midbrain – Level of Inferior Colliculus

etymology.story: The trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique, whose tendon passes through a pulley (trochlea).

info.explanation: Somatic motor nucleus in the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus.

facts.function: Innervates the contralateral superior oblique.
facts.supply: Superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries.
facts.lesion: Vertical or oblique diplopia from weakness of the opposite eye's superior oblique (the trochlear fibres cross before they exit); the head tilts away from the weak eye, which for a nuclear lesion is toward the side of the lesion.

name: Decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle

lists.group: Caudal Midbrain – Level of Inferior Colliculus

roots.meaning: to cross in an X shape

etymology.story: Decussis is the Roman numeral X (ten), so decussate means to cross in an X pattern.

info.explanation: Crossing of dentatorubrothalamic fibres at the level of the inferior colliculus.

facts.function: Crosses cerebellar output to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus.
facts.supply: Paramedian branches of the basilar and superior cerebellar artery.
facts.lesion: Lesion causes ipsilateral cerebellar signs only before the decussation.

lists.group: Rostral Pons – Level of Trigeminal Nerve

etymology.literal: motor nucleus of the triplet nerve
etymology.story: Trigeminus means "three twins", the triple branches.

info.explanation: Branchial motor nucleus in the mid pons, medial to the principal sensory nucleus.

facts.function: Innervates the muscles of mastication and tensor tympani.
facts.supply: Pontine perforators from the basilar artery.
facts.lesion: Jaw deviates toward the weak side on opening; weakness of chewing.
facts.connections: Bilateral corticobulbar input.

lists.group: Rostral Pons – Level of Trigeminal Nerve

etymology.story: The main trigeminal sensory nucleus.

info.explanation: Pontine nucleus lateral to the motor nucleus receiving discriminative touch from the face.

facts.function: Fine touch and vibration of the face.
facts.lesion: Loss of facial light touch.
facts.connections: Second-order neurons project to VPM thalamus.

lists.group: Rostral Pons – Level of Trigeminal Nerve
Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus
In mid-sagittal / longitudinal section of brainstem

etymology.story: Run longitudinally through the basis pontis.

info.explanation: Descending corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine fibres in the basis pontis.

facts.function: Carry cortical output through the pons.
facts.supply: Pontine perforators from the basilar artery.
facts.lesion: Locked-in syndrome and pure motor stroke.

lists.group: Rostral Pons – Level of Trigeminal Nerve
Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus

etymology.story: Nucleus means kernel (nucula, a little nut).

info.explanation: Large scattered neuronal clusters in the basis pontis.

facts.function: Relay between cerebral cortex and contralateral cerebellum.
facts.passes: Receive corticopontine fibres; their axons form transverse fibres.
facts.connections: Cortex -> pontine nuclei -> contralateral cerebellum via MCP.

lists.group: Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus

etymology.story: The nerve abducts the eye (leads it away from the midline).

info.explanation: Somatic motor nucleus in the caudal pons within the facial colliculus.

facts.function: Innervates ipsilateral lateral rectus and internuclear neurons to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus.
facts.lesion: Nuclear lesion gives ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy; nerve lesion only abduction deficit with esotropia.
facts.connections: Surrounded by the PPRF.

lists.group: Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus

etymology.story: Facies means face.

info.explanation: Branchial motor nucleus in the caudal pons lateral to the abducens.

facts.function: Innervates muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid and posterior digastric.
facts.passes: Facial nerve loops around the abducens nucleus.
facts.lesion: Upper motor neuron lesion spares the forehead; lower motor neuron lesion (Bell palsy) paralyses the whole side.
facts.connections: Upper facial: bilateral cortical input; lower facial: contralateral input.

lists.group: Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus

etymology.story: Vestibulum is Latin for a forecourt or entrance hall; cochlea is Greek kochlias, "snail".

info.explanation: Group of vestibular and cochlear nuclei at the pontomedullary junction.

facts.function: Processes balance and hearing information.
facts.lesion: Vestibulocochlear lesion gives vertigo, nystagmus and deafness.
facts.connections: Cochlear nuclei project to the superior olive and lateral lemniscus.

lists.group: Caudal Pons – Level of Facial Colliculus
Cranial nerves I-VIII, IX/X, and XII on a wet specimen
Cranial nerves I-XII on an image or schematic

etymology.story: CN VII; mostly supplies the face.

info.explanation: Cranial nerve VII carrying motor to facial expression, parasympathetic to salivary and lacrimal glands, and taste from anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

facts.function: Facial expression, tears, saliva, taste and ear sensation.
facts.passes: Internal acoustic meatus, facial canal, stylomastoid foramen.
facts.lesion: Bell palsy (LMN): whole face weak; stroke (UMN): sparing forehead.
facts.connections: Nuclei: facial, superior salivatory and solitary.

etymology.story: The nerve runs under the tongue.

info.explanation: Somatic motor nucleus in the medial medulla beneath the hypoglossal trigone.

facts.function: Innervates all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus.
facts.lesion: Tongue deviates toward the lesion side.

name: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

lists.note: Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (DMV / DMX) Solitary nucleus

etymology.story: Vagus means "wandering" because the nerve wanders from the head to the abdomen (source of "vagabond").

info.explanation: Parasympathetic nucleus in the medulla beneath the vagal trigone.

facts.function: Provides parasympathetic innervation to thoracic and abdominal viscera.
facts.lesion: Loss affects visceral motility and heart rate.

lists.note: Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (DMV / DMX) Solitary nucleus

etymology.story: It surrounds the solitary tract, a bundle that appears isolated in section.

info.explanation: Sensory nucleus in the medulla receiving visceral afferents and taste.

facts.function: Taste (VII, IX, X) and visceral sensation including baroreceptor and chemoreceptor input; gag reflex afferent.
facts.passes: Facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve inputs.
facts.lesion: Wallenberg syndrome: loss of taste and gag reflex.
facts.connections: Projects to VPM thalamus and hypothalamus.

etymology.story: Named because its boundaries are indistinct in section.

info.explanation: Branchial motor nucleus in the lateral medulla.

facts.function: Motor supply of pharynx, soft palate and larynx for swallowing and phonation.
facts.passes: Glossopharyngeal, vagus and cranial accessory fibres.
facts.lesion: Dysphagia, hoarseness, uvula deviating away from the lesion in Wallenberg syndrome.
facts.connections: Bilateral cortical input.

lists.group: In mid-sagittal / longitudinal section of brainstem

etymology.story: Folded nucleus shaped like an olive.

info.explanation: Large nucleus within the medulla forming the olive; sends climbing fibres to the contralateral cerebellum.

facts.function: Motor learning and timing via climbing fibres to Purkinje cells.
facts.passes: Olivocerebellar fibres through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
facts.lesion: Hypertrophic olivary degeneration.
facts.connections: Spinal cord and red nucleus to olive to the cerebellum.

lists.group: Cranial nerves I-VIII, IX/X, and XII on a wet specimen
Cranial nerves I-XII on an image or schematic

etymology.story: CN IX supplies the tongue and pharynx.

info.explanation: Cranial nerve IX that carries motor to stylopharyngeus, parasympathetic to parotid, taste and sensation from the posterior tongue and pharynx, and carotid sinus input.

facts.function: Swallowing, parotid secretion, taste, gag afferent and baroreception.
facts.lesion: Loss of gag reflex and taste on the posterior tongue; glossopharyngeal neuralgia.
facts.connections: Nuclei: nucleus ambiguus, inferior salivatory, solitary.

lists.group: Cranial nerves I-VIII, IX/X, and XII on a wet specimen
Cranial nerves I-XII on an image or schematic

etymology.story: The longest cranial nerve, wandering from the head to the abdomen.

info.explanation: Cranial nerve X giving motor to pharynx and larynx and parasympathetic to thoracic and abdominal viscera.

facts.function: Swallowing, phonation, heart rate, GI motility.
facts.lesion: Hoarseness, dysphagia, uvular deviation away from lesion, bradycardia.
facts.connections: Nuclei: ambiguus, dorsal motor, solitary and spinal trigeminal.

lists.group: Cranial nerves I-VIII, IX/X, and XII on a wet specimen
Cranial nerves I-XII on an image or schematic

etymology.story: CN XII passes beneath the tongue.

info.explanation: Cranial nerve XII innervating all tongue muscles except palatoglossus.

facts.function: Tongue movement for speech and swallowing.
facts.lesion: Tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion.
facts.connections: Nucleus in the medial medulla.

lists.group: Caudal Medulla – Level of Cuneate & Gracile Tubercles

etymology.story: Slender nucleus of the dorsal medulla.

info.explanation: Dorsal medullary nucleus where the fasciculus gracilis synapses.

facts.function: Second-order relay of the DCML for the lower body.
facts.lesion: Loss of lower-body vibration and proprioception.
facts.connections: Axons form internal arcuate fibres and cross.

lists.group: Caudal Medulla – Level of Cuneate & Gracile Tubercles

etymology.story: Wedge-shaped nucleus.

info.explanation: Dorsal medullary nucleus lateral to the nucleus gracilis where the fasciculus cuneatus synapses.

facts.function: Second-order relay of the DCML for the upper body.
facts.lesion: Loss of upper-limb vibration and proprioception.
facts.connections: Axons form internal arcuate fibres and cross.

lists.group: Caudal Medulla – Level of Cuneate & Gracile Tubercles

etymology.story: Arcuate means bow-shaped; the fibres sweep in arcs.

info.explanation: Second-order axons from the gracile and cuneate nuclei sweeping anteromedially and decussating to form the medial lemniscus.

facts.function: Decussation of the DCML in the caudal medulla.
facts.connections: Where the medial lemniscus decussates.

lists.group: Caudal Medulla – Level of Cuneate & Gracile Tubercles

etymology.story: Extends down into the upper cervical cord.

info.explanation: Long nucleus extending from the pons to the upper cervical cord.

facts.function: Pain and temperature from the face and also from the ear and throat.
facts.passes: Trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus afferents.
facts.lesion: Wallenberg: ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss.
facts.connections: Second-order axons cross to VPM thalamus.

etymology.story: Decussis is the Roman X.

info.explanation: Crossing of about 90% of corticospinal fibres at the caudal medulla.

facts.function: Directs most motor control to the opposite side of the body.
facts.lesion: Lesions above cause contralateral weakness; below cause ipsilateral.

etymology.literal: lateral tract from cortex to spinal cord
etymology.story: Named for its origin and target.

info.explanation: Crossed corticospinal tract in the lateral funiculus.

facts.function: Voluntary control of distal limb muscles.
facts.supply: Anterior spinal artery and posterior spinal arteries.
facts.lesion: Ipsilateral UMN signs below the lesion in the cord (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski).
facts.connections: Terminates on ventral horn lower motor neurons.

etymology.literal: anterior tract from cortex to spinal cord
etymology.story: Ventral tract.

info.explanation: Uncrossed corticospinal tract in the anterior funiculus.

facts.function: Controls trunk and proximal muscles bilaterally.
facts.lesion: Mild axial weakness.
facts.connections: Crosses at the segmental level via the anterior white commissure.

etymology.story: Funiculus is a diminutive of funis, "rope".

info.explanation: White matter of the spinal cord lateral to the ventral and dorsal horns.

facts.function: Carries lateral corticospinal, rubrospinal, spinocerebellar and spinothalamic tracts.

etymology.story: Ventral white matter column.

info.explanation: White matter between the ventral median fissure and the ventral root.

facts.function: Carries anterior corticospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal and tectospinal tracts.

name: Location of limb lower motor neurons

etymology.literal: at the side of the horn
etymology.story: Limb muscles sit far from the body axis, so their motor neurons sit far from the midline, in the lateral ventral horn (lateral = Latin latus, side). Position in the cord mirrors position in the body.

info.explanation: Lower motor neurons for limb muscles lie in the lateral part of the ventral horn at the cervical and lumbosacral enlargements.

facts.function: Control limb muscles.
facts.connections: Distal muscles are most lateral; flexors are posterior.

name: Location of trunk lower motor neurons

etymology.literal: in the middle of the horn
etymology.story: Trunk and axial muscles lie near the body midline, and their motor neurons sit correspondingly medial in the ventral horn (medial = Latin medius, middle).

info.explanation: Lower motor neurons for axial and trunk muscles lie medially in the ventral horn.

facts.function: Control the trunk and proximal musculature.

etymology.story: From pro (forward) and tuber (swelling): a bump.

info.explanation: Ventral bulge of the basis pontis.

facts.function: Contains pontine nuclei and corticopontine fibres.
facts.lesion: Basilar occlusion infarcts.

etymology.story: Cornea tela, "horny tissue", from cornu, horn, because it is tough and translucent like horn.

info.explanation: Transparent avascular anterior covering of the eye, the major refractive surface.

facts.function: Refracts light (about two-thirds of the eye's focusing power) and protects the eye.
facts.supply: Avascular; oxygen from tears and aqueous humour.
facts.lesion: Corneal reflex tests CN V1 (afferent) and CN VII (efferent).

etymology.story: Skleros means hard, the same root as "sclerosis".

info.explanation: White opaque outer coat of the eye.

facts.function: Gives the eye its shape and protects it; extraocular muscles insert here.

lists.group: Cranial nerves I-VIII, IX/X, and XII on a wet specimen
Cranial nerves I-XII on an image or schematic

etymology.story: Optikos is Greek for "relating to sight".

info.explanation: CN II, formed by retinal ganglion cell axons; technically a CNS tract.

facts.function: Carries visual information to the chiasm.
facts.lesion: Optic neuritis (multiple sclerosis) causes monocular vision loss and relative afferent pupillary defect; papilloedema.
facts.connections: Ganglion cells -> optic nerve -> chiasm.

etymology.story: Radiations are fibres that fan out like rays.

info.explanation: Fibres from the LGN to V1; Meyer loop carries the upper visual field, the parietal route the lower field.

facts.function: Carries visual information to V1.
facts.supply: Middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery.
facts.lesion: Temporal lobe lesion: contralateral upper quadrantanopia (pie in the sky); parietal lobe lesion: lower quadrantanopia.
facts.connections: LGN -> V1.

etymology.story: Iris was the Greek goddess of the rainbow, and the coloured disc resembles one.

info.explanation: Pigmented muscular diaphragm of the eye surrounding the pupil.

facts.function: Controls pupil size: sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic) constricts, dilator pupillae (sympathetic) dilates.
facts.lesion: Horner syndrome causes miosis; CN III palsy causes mydriasis.

etymology.story: Latin lens is the lentil, a lens-shaped seed; the optical lens was named after the legume, not the reverse.

info.explanation: Transparent biconvex structure behind the iris that fine-focuses light.

facts.function: Accommodation by the ciliary muscle changing its shape.
facts.lesion: Cataract (clouding) and presbyopia.

etymology.story: From rete, net, either from its network of vessels or because it was thought to be like a fisherman's net.

info.explanation: Light-sensitive neural layer lining the back of the eye containing rods, cones, bipolar and ganglion cells.

facts.function: Transduces light into neural signals.
facts.lesion: Retinal detachment, central retinal artery occlusion (cherry-red spot), diabetic retinopathy.
facts.connections: Photoreceptors -> bipolar -> ganglion cells -> optic nerve.

etymology.story: Named by analogy with the chorion, because of its rich vessels.

info.explanation: Vascular, pigmented layer between the retina and sclera.

facts.function: Nourishes the outer retina and absorbs stray light.
facts.lesion: Choroidal melanoma; choroiditis.

etymology.story: It lies directly above the optic chiasm.

info.explanation: Small hypothalamic nucleus above the optic chiasm.

facts.function: Master circadian clock, entrained by light through the retinohypothalamic tract.
facts.lesion: Disrupted sleep-wake cycle.
facts.connections: Projects to pineal via sympathetic route.

lists.note: Know that PPRF (lateral gaze center) surrounds Abducens nucleus

etymology.story: Reticulum is a little net; the reticular formation looks like a diffuse net of cells.

info.explanation: Pontine region beside the midline around the abducens nucleus (horizontal gaze centre).

facts.function: Generates ipsilateral horizontal saccades.
facts.passes: Projects to the ipsilateral abducens nucleus.
facts.lesion: Lesion causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy.
facts.connections: Abducens nucleus and PPRF together form the lateral gaze centre.

etymology.story: Insula is Latin for island: the cortex lies buried in the lateral fissure like an island, also known as the Island of Reil.

info.explanation: Cortex buried deep in the lateral fissure, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula.

facts.function: Taste (gustatory cortex), visceral sensation, pain, interoception and autonomic regulation.
facts.lesion: Insular stroke: dysgeusia, autonomic dysfunction, speech apraxia; can mimic cardiac pain or alter heart rhythm.
facts.connections: Receives from the ventral posteromedial thalamus.

etymology.story: Genu means knee (as in "genuflect", to bend the knee): the front of the corpus callosum bends like a knee.

info.explanation: Anterior bend of the corpus callosum connecting the frontal lobes via the forceps minor.

facts.function: Interhemispheric transfer between the prefrontal cortices.
facts.supply: Anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal and callosomarginal branches).
facts.lesion: Frontal disconnection syndromes.

etymology.story: Corpus means body: the body is the long middle part.

info.explanation: Long central part of the corpus callosum forming the roof of the lateral ventricle.

facts.function: Interhemispheric transfer between frontal, parietal and temporal areas.
facts.lesion: Callosotomy for epilepsy causes disconnection syndrome.

etymology.story: Splenion is Greek for a bandage or compress, because the thickened posterior end looks like a roll of bandage.

info.explanation: Thick posterior end of the corpus callosum connecting occipital and temporal lobes via the forceps major.

facts.function: Interhemispheric transfer of visual information.
facts.supply: Posterior pericallosal branches of the posterior cerebral artery; also ACA.
facts.lesion: Alexia without agraphia from a lesion of the splenium and left occipital cortex.

etymology.story: Named for its long tapering tail curving around the thalamus.

info.explanation: C-shaped nucleus along the lateral wall of the lateral ventricle with a head, body and tail.

facts.function: Receives cortical input for motor, cognitive and limbic loops; with the putamen forms the striatum.
facts.supply: Lenticulostriate arteries, medial striate artery (Heubner) and anterior choroidal artery.
facts.lesion: Huntington disease (atrophy of the caudate); OCD; abulia after caudate infarcts.
facts.connections: Cortex -> caudate -> GPi/SNr -> thalamus -> cortex.

etymology.story: Caput means head.

info.explanation: Large rounded anterior part of the caudate bulging into the anterior horn of the lateral ventricle.

facts.function: Cognitive and limbic corticostriatal loops.
facts.supply: Lenticulostriate and recurrent artery of Heubner.
facts.lesion: Atrophy in Huntington disease enlarges the frontal horns.
facts.connections: Forms the lateral wall of the anterior horn.

etymology.story: Corpus means body.

info.explanation: Narrow central part of the caudate on the floor of the lateral ventricle body above the thalamus.

facts.function: Corticostriatal loops.

etymology.story: The tail follows the lateral ventricle into the temporal lobe.

info.explanation: Thin tail of the caudate curving into the temporal lobe, ending near the amygdala.

facts.function: Corticostriatal visual and auditory loops.
facts.connections: Ends at the amygdala.

roots.meaning: that which is pruned off, husk, shell

etymology.story: Putamen is Latin for the shell or husk removed when pruning, from putare "to prune"; it forms the outer shell of the lentiform nucleus.

info.explanation: Large lateral nucleus of the lentiform nucleus; with the caudate forms the striatum.

facts.function: Motor loop: cortex -> putamen -> GPi -> VL thalamus -> motor cortex.
facts.lesion: Parkinson disease, Huntington disease, hemiballismus; hypertensive haemorrhage commonly here.
facts.connections: Receives from motor cortex and substantia nigra.

etymology.story: Pallidus is Latin for pale: the nucleus is paler than the putamen because it is traversed by many myelinated axons.

info.explanation: Medial part of the lentiform nucleus, divided into external (GPe) and internal (GPi) segments.

facts.function: Output of the basal ganglia: GPi inhibits thalamus (VL).
facts.lesion: Lesions cause dystonia; deep brain stimulation target for Parkinson disease.
facts.connections: Putamen -> GPe/GPi -> thalamus and subthalamic nucleus.

etymology.story: The internal capsule fibres run through the caudate and putamen creating a striped appearance.

info.explanation: Collective name for caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus joined by grey bridges through the anterior limb of the internal capsule.

facts.function: Basal ganglia input and output structures.
facts.lesion: Basal ganglia diseases.

lists.note: Lentiform (lens shaped) nucleus is composed of Putamen and Globus pallidus

etymology.story: Named for its lentil/lens shape in horizontal sections.

info.explanation: Putamen plus globus pallidus, forming a lens-shaped mass lateral to the internal capsule.

facts.function: Motor control.
facts.lesion: Hemorrhage and lacunes.
facts.connections: Lateral to the internal capsule.

etymology.literal: front leg of the inner capsule
etymology.story: Crus means leg; the internal capsule has an anterior leg, genu (knee) and posterior leg.

info.explanation: Part of the internal capsule between the caudate head and the lentiform nucleus.

facts.function: Carries frontopontine and anterior thalamic radiation fibres.
facts.passes: Frontopontine fibres and anterior thalamic radiations.
facts.supply: Lenticulostriate arteries (MCA) and recurrent artery of Heubner (ACA).
facts.lesion: Lesions cause abulia and executive deficits.

etymology.story: Genu means knee (hence "genuflect").

info.explanation: Bend of the internal capsule between the anterior and posterior limbs at the foramen of Monro.

facts.function: Contains corticobulbar fibres.
facts.supply: Branches of the internal carotid artery and anterior choroidal artery.
facts.lesion: Contralateral weakness of the lower face, tongue and dysarthria.

etymology.literal: back leg of the inner capsule
etymology.story: Crus is leg.

info.explanation: Part of the internal capsule between the thalamus and lentiform nucleus.

facts.function: Carries corticospinal fibres and thalamocortical sensory radiations.
facts.passes: Corticospinal fibres (arm anterior, leg posterior), thalamocortical somatosensory fibres, optic and auditory radiations in its retrolenticular and sublenticular parts.
facts.supply: As taught: lenticulostriate branches (MCA), PCA deep branches to the posterior limb; classically also the anterior choroidal artery.
facts.lesion: Pure motor hemiparesis or pure sensory stroke (lacunar syndrome).

info.review_note: Course slide credits PCA deep branches for the posterior limb; textbooks also give lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal arteries. Check against the lecture.

etymology.story: Fornix is the Latin word for an arch or vaulted chamber; the Roman brothels were in vaulted arches, which gave us "fornication".

info.explanation: C-shaped white matter tract arching from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies.

facts.function: Memory pathway of the limbic system (Papez circuit).
facts.supply: Posterior cerebral artery and anterior choroidal artery.
facts.lesion: Damage causes anterograde amnesia.
facts.connections: Hippocampus -> fornix -> mammillary bodies.

etymology.story: The fornix has crura (legs) that diverge posteriorly.

info.explanation: Posterior continuation of the fornix as it separates from the splenium of the corpus callosum.

facts.function: Carries hippocampal output.
facts.lesion: Memory impairment.
facts.connections: Continues from the fimbria.

etymology.story: Fused midline part under the corpus callosum.

info.explanation: Midline portion where the two crura merge under the corpus callosum.

facts.function: Carries hippocampal fibres.
facts.connections: Forms part of the septum pellucidum floor.

etymology.story: Columna means pillar.

info.explanation: Anterior descending arches of the fornix that curve in front of the foramen of Monro to the mammillary bodies.

facts.function: Carry hippocampal efferents to the mammillary bodies and septal nuclei.
facts.lesion: Surgical damage (colloid cyst removal) causes amnesia.
facts.connections: Forms the anterior boundary of the foramen of Monro.

etymology.story: It is the thin plate that closes the anterior neuropore, the rostral end of the neural tube.

info.explanation: Thin membrane forming the rostral wall of the third ventricle between the optic chiasm and anterior commissure.

facts.function: Closes the anterior end of the third ventricle.
facts.lesion: Anterior communicating aneurysms may abut it; opened surgically in third ventriculostomy.
facts.connections: Contains the OVLT (circumventricular organ).

etymology.story: Stria means streak; medullaris refers to the medulla, white marrow.

info.explanation: White matter tract along the dorsomedial thalamus, carrying input to the habenula.

facts.function: Links the septal and limbic structures with the habenula.

etymology.story: Habena is a strap or rein; the habenula looks like a small bridle or rein.

info.explanation: Small nucleus at the posterior end of the stria medullaris in the epithalamus.

facts.function: Links limbic forebrain to midbrain (reward, aversion).
facts.passes: Stria medullaris; fasciculus retroflexus to interpeduncular nucleus.
facts.lesion: Implicated in depression.
facts.connections: Input from the stria medullaris; output via fasciculus retroflexus.

etymology.story: Commissure is a joining or crossing bundle.

info.explanation: White matter bundle crossing the midline at the junction of the midbrain and third ventricle above the cerebral aqueduct.

facts.function: Pupillary light reflex (consensual response), upgaze.
facts.lesion: Parinaud syndrome: upgaze palsy and light-near dissociation.

lists.note: Cortical Ribbon or Cortical gray matter

etymology.story: The grey matter forms a ribbon-like layer in imaging.

info.explanation: Thin sheet of grey matter at the brain surface, seen as the cortical ribbon on imaging.

facts.function: Houses neuronal cell bodies.
facts.lesion: Cortical ribbon sign on DWI indicates infarct or Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

etymology.literal: nuclei at the base of the forebrain
etymology.story: Located beneath the basal ganglia at the base of the forebrain.

info.explanation: Group including the septal nuclei and nucleus basalis of Meynert.

facts.function: Provide cholinergic input to the cortex (memory, attention).
facts.supply: Anterior cerebral and communicating artery branches.
facts.lesion: Degeneration in Alzheimer disease.
facts.connections: Project to cortex and hippocampus.

etymology.story: Accumbens means "reclining against", because it lies against the septum pellucidum.

info.explanation: Ventral striatum where the head of the caudate meets the putamen.

facts.function: Reward, motivation, addiction.
facts.lesion: Implicated in addiction and depression.
facts.connections: Receives dopamine from the ventral tegmental area.

etymology.story: Lies beneath the thalamus.

info.explanation: Lens-shaped excitatory nucleus beneath the thalamus, part of the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia.

facts.function: Excitatory drive to the globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra reticulata.
facts.supply: Posterior communicating and posterior cerebral arteries.
facts.lesion: Hemiballismus: violent flinging of the contralateral limbs; deep brain stimulation target in Parkinson disease.
facts.connections: Globus pallidus externus -> STN -> GPi.

etymology.story: Tonsilla is a diminutive of tonsa, "a stake"; the cerebellar tonsil is a small rounded lobule near the foramen magnum.

info.explanation: Rounded lobule on the inferior cerebellum next to the medulla.

facts.function: Part of the cerebellar hemisphere.
facts.lesion: Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses the medulla; Chiari I malformation.

etymology.story: Floccus is Latin for a tuft of wool (also in "flocculent").

info.explanation: Small lobule of the flocculonodular lobe next to the middle cerebellar peduncle.

facts.function: Vestibulo-ocular reflex and eye movements.
facts.lesion: Gaze-evoked nystagmus.
facts.connections: Part of vestibulocerebellum.

etymology.story: Vermis is Latin for worm, because the midline cerebellum looks like a worm.

info.explanation: Midline strip of the cerebellum.

facts.function: Controls axial and trunk balance and posture.
facts.lesion: Truncal ataxia, wide-based gait.
facts.connections: Output via fastigial nucleus.

etymology.story: Lies on either side of the vermis.

info.explanation: Region lateral to the vermis, also called the intermediate zone.

facts.function: Controls distal limb movements.
facts.lesion: Ipsilateral limb ataxia.
facts.connections: Output via the interposed nuclei.

etymology.story: Hemisphere means half of a sphere.

info.explanation: Large lateral part of the cerebellar hemisphere.

facts.function: Planning and coordination of skilled limb movements.
facts.lesion: Ipsilateral dysmetria and intention tremor.
facts.connections: Output via dentate nucleus.

etymology.story: Named for the zigzag, tooth-like edge of its folded grey matter.

info.explanation: Largest deep cerebellar nucleus in the lateral hemisphere.

facts.function: Main output of the cerebellum to the thalamus and red nucleus.
facts.lesion: Ipsilateral limb ataxia and tremor.
facts.connections: Output to the contralateral VL thalamus.

etymology.story: Arteria originally meant windpipe: arteries were thought to carry air because they were empty in the dead.

info.explanation: Arise from the subclavian arteries, ascend through the transverse foramina of C6-C1, enter through the foramen magnum.

facts.supply: Supply the brainstem, cerebellum and posterior cerebrum.
facts.lesion: Occlusion causes Wallenberg syndrome; dissection after neck trauma.
facts.connections: Join to form the basilar artery. Origin / part of: Posterior circulation.

etymology.story: Runs along the base of the brainstem.

info.explanation: Formed by union of the vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction.

facts.supply: Supplies the pons, cerebellum and occipital lobes.
facts.lesion: Basilar occlusion: locked-in syndrome.
facts.connections: Terminates as the posterior cerebral arteries. Origin / part of: Posterior circulation.

lists.note: Cerebellar branches (three pairs supply cerebellum) – only ID for Superior Cerebellar Artery

etymology.story: Supplies the cerebellum's superior surface.

info.explanation: Branch of the basilar artery just below the PCA.

facts.supply: Supplies the superior cerebellum, dentate and rostral pons.
facts.lesion: Ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia.
facts.connections: Separated from the PCA by CN III. Origin / part of: Basilar artery.

name: Penetrating branches (brainstem)
synonyms: perforating branches of the basilar artery

etymology.story: Small branches pierce the brainstem directly.

info.explanation: Short paramedian and long circumferential arteries that penetrate the brainstem.

facts.lesion: Small-vessel strokes cause brainstem syndromes.
facts.connections: Origin / part of: Basilar and vertebral arteries.

etymology.story: Branches to the pons.

info.explanation: Small branches of the basilar artery supplying the pons.

facts.lesion: Pontine infarct, locked-in syndrome.
facts.connections: Origin / part of: Basilar artery.

etymology.story: Supplies the posterior cerebrum.

info.explanation: Terminal branch of the basilar artery supplying the occipital lobe and inferior temporal lobe.

facts.supply: Supplies visual cortex, inferior temporal lobe and thalamus.
facts.lesion: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing; visual agnosia.
facts.connections: Origin / part of: Basilar artery.

etymology.story: Communicans connects arteries, from communicare "to share".

info.explanation: Links the internal carotid artery with the posterior cerebral artery.

facts.supply: Joins anterior and posterior circulations in the circle of Willis.
facts.lesion: Aneurysm compresses CN III: ptosis, blown pupil.
facts.connections: Origin / part of: ICA and PCA.

etymology.story: Greek karos means "heavy sleep"; compressing the carotids causes loss of consciousness.

info.explanation: Enters through the carotid canal and gives off ophthalmic, anterior and middle cerebral arteries.

facts.supply: Supplies the anterior circulation: frontal, parietal, and part of the temporal lobes and the eye.
facts.lesion: Amaurosis fugax; carotid stenosis causes stroke.
facts.connections: Origin / part of: Common carotid artery.

etymology.story: Largest branch of the internal carotid.

info.explanation: Largest branch of the ICA; runs in the lateral fissure.

facts.supply: Supplies lateral cerebral cortex, including motor and sensory face and arm areas, and language areas.
facts.lesion: Contralateral face and arm weakness, aphasia (left), hemineglect (right).
facts.connections: Gives lenticulostriate branches. Origin / part of: ICA.

lists.note: Lenticulostriate Arteries penetrating Anterior Perforated Substance

etymology.story: They supply the lentiform nucleus and striatum.

info.explanation: Small perforating branches of the MCA entering the anterior perforated substance.

facts.supply: Supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule.
facts.lesion: Lacunar infarcts; hypertensive hemorrhage (Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms).
facts.connections: Origin / part of: MCA.

etymology.story: Supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes.

info.explanation: Branch of the ICA running over the corpus callosum.

facts.supply: Supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes, with leg motor and sensory areas.
facts.lesion: Contralateral leg weakness, abulia.
facts.connections: Origin / part of: ICA.

etymology.story: Peri- means "around".

info.explanation: Continuation of the ACA around the corpus callosum.

facts.supply: Supplies the corpus callosum and medial hemispheres.
facts.lesion: Callosal infarct.
facts.connections: Origin / part of: ACA.

etymology.story: It runs in the cingulate sulcus above the pericallosal artery.

info.explanation: Branch of the ACA in the cingulate sulcus.

facts.supply: Supplies the cingulate and paracentral areas.
facts.lesion: Infarct causes leg weakness.
facts.connections: Origin / part of: ACA.

etymology.story: It connects the two anterior cerebral arteries.

info.explanation: Short vessel linking the two ACAs.

facts.lesion: Most common site of berry aneurysm; rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage.
facts.connections: Origin / part of: ACAs.

etymology.story: Named for the English physician Thomas Willis, who described it in 1664 and coined the word "neurology".

info.explanation: Anastomotic ring of arteries at the base of the brain linking the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems.

facts.lesion: Berry aneurysms.
facts.connections: Origin / part of: ICA, ACA, AComA, PComA, PCA.

etymology.story: Midline vessel on the ventral cord.

info.explanation: Formed by branches of the vertebral arteries, running along the ventral median fissure.

facts.supply: Supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord.
facts.lesion: Anterior spinal artery syndrome: bilateral loss of motor and pain/temperature, sparing dorsal columns.
facts.connections: Fed by radicular arteries, including the artery of Adamkiewicz. Origin / part of: Vertebral arteries.

lists.note: Posterior spinal arteries (only in a picture)

etymology.story: Paired posterolateral vessels.

info.explanation: Paired arteries running along the dorsolateral sulci.

facts.supply: Supply the posterior one-third of the spinal cord.
facts.lesion: Loss of vibration and proprioception.
facts.connections: Origin / part of: Vertebral or PICA.

etymology.story: Imago, "likeness", also gave "imagine" and "image".

info.explanation: Neuroimaging techniques such as CT, MRI (T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI), MRA, CTA and PET.

facts.function: CT shows acute blood (hyperdense) and bone quickly; MRI gives soft tissue contrast; DWI detects acute ischaemia within minutes.

etymology.story: Haemorrhage comes from Greek haima "blood" and rhegnynai "to burst forth".

info.explanation: Intracranial haemorrhage types: epidural, subdural, subarachnoid and intraparenchymal.

facts.function: Distinguished by location and CT shape: epidural lens-shaped, subdural crescent-shaped, subarachnoid blood in cisterns and sulci.
facts.supply: Epidural: middle meningeal artery; subdural: bridging veins; subarachnoid: berry aneurysm; intraparenchymal: hypertensive small vessels.
facts.lesion: Epidural: lucid interval; subdural: elderly, shaken infants, alcohol; subarachnoid: thunderclap headache.

lists.group: Cranial nerves I-VIII, IX/X, and XII on a wet specimen
Cranial nerves I-XII on an image or schematic

etymology.story: Olfacere combines olere "to emit an odour" and facere "to make".

info.explanation: Cranial nerve I: bundles of axons of olfactory receptor neurons passing through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb.

facts.function: Smell.
facts.lesion: Anosmia after head trauma or fracture of the cribriform plate; Kallmann syndrome.
facts.connections: Unique: no thalamic relay.

lists.group: Cranial nerves I-VIII, IX/X, and XII on a wet specimen
Cranial nerves I-XII on an image or schematic

etymology.story: CN IV: its muscle, the superior oblique, loops through a pulley; early anatomists called it the "pathetic nerve" because the muscle expresses emotion in sidelong glances.

info.explanation: Cranial nerve IV supplying the superior oblique; the only cranial nerve that exits dorsally and crosses.

facts.function: Intorsion and depression of the adducted eye.
facts.lesion: Vertical diplopia on looking down (reading, stairs); head tilt away.
facts.connections: Smallest nerve; longest intracranial course.

lists.group: Cranial nerves I-VIII, IX/X, and XII on a wet specimen
Cranial nerves I-XII on an image or schematic

etymology.story: Three divisions (V1, V2, V3).

info.explanation: Cranial nerve V with three sensory divisions (ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular) and motor fibres to the muscles of mastication.

facts.function: Facial sensation and chewing.
facts.passes: V1 superior orbital fissure; V2 foramen rotundum; V3 foramen ovale.
facts.lesion: Trigeminal neuralgia; corneal reflex loss.
facts.connections: Nuclei: mesencephalic, principal, spinal, motor.

lists.group: Cranial nerves I-VIII, IX/X, and XII on a wet specimen
Cranial nerves I-XII on an image or schematic

etymology.story: CN VI abducts the eye.

info.explanation: Cranial nerve VI supplying the lateral rectus.

facts.function: Abduction of the eye.
facts.lesion: Medial deviation of the eye and horizontal diplopia; long course makes it vulnerable to raised intracranial pressure.
facts.connections: Nucleus lies in the facial colliculus.

lists.group: Cranial nerves I-VIII, IX/X, and XII on a wet specimen
Cranial nerves I-XII on an image or schematic

etymology.literal: nerve of the hall and snail
etymology.story: Combines the vestibular system (balance) and the snail-shaped cochlea (hearing).

info.explanation: Cranial nerve VIII carrying hearing and balance from the inner ear.

facts.function: Hearing and balance.
facts.lesion: Vestibular schwannoma: hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo.
facts.connections: Nuclei at pontomedullary junction.

lists.group: Cranial nerves I-XII on an image or schematic
lists.note: Accessory nerve is not present on our brainstems

etymology.story: Originally considered an accessory (extra) to the vagus.

info.explanation: Cranial nerve XI: spinal root from C1-C5 supplying sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.

facts.function: Turning the head and shrugging shoulders.
facts.lesion: Weakness of shoulder shrug (trapezius) and head turn away from the lesion (SCM).
facts.connections: Spinal accessory nucleus in the cervical cord.

roots.meaning: lobe, lower part of the ear

etymology.story: The lobe lies beneath the frontal bone of the forehead. Lobe comes from Greek lobos, a rounded projecting part.

info.explanation: The most anterior cerebral lobe, bounded behind by the central sulcus and below by the lateral fissure. It contains motor, premotor and prefrontal cortex.

facts.function: Voluntary movement, speech production, executive function and behavior

etymology.story: Named for the parietal bone of the skull, itself named as a wall of the cranium.

info.explanation: The cerebral lobe between the central sulcus and the parieto-occipital fissure, above the lateral fissure. It houses somatosensory cortex and association areas for spatial processing.

facts.function: Somatosensation, spatial awareness, integration of sensory information

etymology.literal: lobe of the back of the head
etymology.story: Occiput, the back of the head, is from ob (behind) plus caput (head). The lobe lies under the occipital bone.

info.explanation: The most posterior cerebral lobe, containing primary visual cortex around the calcarine fissure and visual association areas.

facts.function: Processing of visual information

etymology.story: Lies beneath the temporal bone at the temple, the side of the head.

info.explanation: The cerebral lobe below the lateral fissure. It contains primary auditory cortex, Wernicke's area, and (medially) the hippocampus and amygdala.

facts.function: Hearing, language comprehension, memory and emotion

etymology.story: Greek gyros, circle, passed through Latin gyrus; a gyrus is a rounded ridge of cortex.

info.explanation: A raised fold of cerebral cortex lying between two sulci. Folding into gyri and sulci greatly increases cortical surface area.

etymology.story: Latin sulcus is a furrow plowed in a field; a sulcus is a groove in the cortex.

info.explanation: A shallow groove on the cerebral surface separating adjacent gyri. A deeper sulcus is called a fissure.

etymology.literal: flowing fluid of the brain and spine
etymology.story: The fluid bathes both the brain and the spinal cord.

info.explanation: A clear fluid made mainly by the choroid plexus that fills the ventricles and subarachnoid space, cushioning the CNS. It is reabsorbed into venous blood via arachnoid granulations.

facts.function: Cushioning, buoyancy and chemical stability of the CNS
facts.passes: Lateral ventricles, interventricular foramina, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, subarachnoid space

etymology.story: The English word descends from Old English brægen. The Greek-derived medical term encephalon means 'in the head'.

info.explanation: The part of the central nervous system within the skull, made up of the cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem and cerebellum, and protected by bone, meninges and CSF.

etymology.story: Humor is Latin for fluid; ancient medicine spoke of the body's four humors.

info.explanation: A watery fluid filling the anterior and posterior chambers in front of the lens, nourishing the cornea and lens and maintaining eye pressure.

facts.function: Nourishes the lens and cornea; maintains intraocular pressure

etymology.story: The clear, jelly-like mass looks like glass.

info.explanation: A transparent gel filling the large chamber behind the lens and in front of the retina, holding the retina in place and maintaining the shape of the eye.

etymology.story: Looking into someone's pupil you see a tiny reflection of yourself, a 'little doll'. Pupilla is a diminutive of pupa, girl or doll.

info.explanation: The central opening in the iris through which light enters the eye. Its size is controlled by the sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic, via CN III) and dilator pupillae (sympathetic).

facts.function: Regulates the amount of light reaching the retina

etymology.story: In horizontal sections the large mass of hemispheric white matter above the lateral ventricles looks like a half-oval.

info.explanation: The large region of white matter in each hemisphere above the corpus callosum and lateral ventricle, formed by corona radiata, callosal and association fibers.

etymology.story: Myelin, a fatty sheath, gives axon bundles a pale color in fresh tissue.

info.explanation: Myelinated axons that connect regions of the CNS, forming projection, commissural and association fibers. Cell bodies are found in gray matter instead.

facts.function: Conducts signals between brain regions and between brain and spinal cord

etymology.literal: white substance of the little brain (arbor vitae)
etymology.story: In sagittal section the white matter branches like a tree, called the arbor vitae, 'tree of life'.

info.explanation: The core of white matter beneath the cerebellar cortex, carrying input to and output from the cortex and surrounding the deep cerebellar nuclei.

etymology.story: Cerebellum is the diminutive of cerebrum; the cortex is the thin folded gray outer layer.

info.explanation: The thin, tightly folded gray matter surface of the cerebellum, organized in three layers (molecular, Purkinje cell, granular). Purkinje cell axons project to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

etymology.story: Nucleus is a Latin diminutive of nux (nut), a kernel of gray matter inside white matter.

info.explanation: Four pairs of gray matter nuclei within the cerebellar white matter: dentate, interposed (emboliform and globose) and fastigial. They send the cerebellar output to the rest of the brain.

facts.connections: Receive Purkinje cell input from the cerebellar cortex; project via the cerebellar peduncles

roots.meaning: gable, peak of a roof, summit

etymology.story: It lies near the fastigium, the apex of the roof of the fourth ventricle.

info.explanation: The most medial deep cerebellar nucleus, receiving input from the vermis and flocculonodular lobe and influencing vestibular and reticular nuclei for posture and balance.

etymology.story: They lie between the fastigial and dentate nuclei. They comprise the emboliform and globose nuclei.

info.explanation: Deep cerebellar nuclei between the fastigial and dentate nuclei, receiving input from the paravermis (intermediate zone) and projecting mainly to the red nucleus.

etymology.literal: lobe of the little tuft and little knot
etymology.story: It consists of the flocculus (little tuft) and nodulus (little knot).

info.explanation: The smallest and phylogenetically oldest cerebellar lobe (flocculi plus nodulus), linked with vestibular nuclei for balance and eye movements.

facts.function: Balance and vestibulo-ocular control

etymology.story: Lies in front of the primary fissure.

info.explanation: The part of the cerebellum rostral to the primary fissure, mostly spinocerebellar, involved in coordination of the limbs and trunk.

etymology.story: Lies behind the primary fissure and in front of the posterolateral fissure.

info.explanation: The largest part of the cerebellum, between the primary and posterolateral fissures, mostly cerebrocerebellar and involved in coordination and planning of movement.

etymology.story: Diminutive of nodus, knot.

info.explanation: The most ventral part of the vermis, forming with the flocculi the flocculonodular lobe for vestibular function.

etymology.story: It lies between the telencephalon and the midbrain.

info.explanation: Part of the forebrain formed from the prosencephalon, comprising the thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus and subthalamus, and the retina via the eye cup.

etymology.story: The most rostral part of the developing brain.

info.explanation: The most rostral brain vesicle derivative of the prosencephalon, forming the cerebral hemispheres, basal ganglia and lateral ventricles.

etymology.story: The most rostral of the three primary brain vesicles.

info.explanation: The embryonic forebrain vesicle that divides into the telencephalon and diencephalon.

etymology.story: Named for the rhomboid shape of the floor of the fourth ventricle.

info.explanation: The embryonic hindbrain vesicle that divides into the metencephalon (pons and cerebellum) and myelencephalon (medulla).

etymology.story: It lies behind the midbrain in the hindbrain.

info.explanation: The rostral part of the rhombencephalon that gives rise to the pons and cerebellum.

etymology.story: The early CNS forms by folding of the neural plate into a tube.

info.explanation: The embryonic precursor of the CNS. Its rostral end forms the brain vesicles and the rest the spinal cord, while its lumen becomes the ventricular system and central canal.

etymology.story: Ventriculus is a diminutive of venter, belly: a small cavity.

info.explanation: The connected CSF-filled cavities of the brain: two lateral ventricles, the third ventricle, the cerebral aqueduct and the fourth ventricle, leading to the subarachnoid space and central canal.

etymology.literal: hollows for blood within the hard (mother)
etymology.story: They are channels between layers of the dura mater.

info.explanation: Endothelium-lined venous channels within the dura that collect blood from the brain and reabsorbed CSF and drain mainly to the internal jugular veins.

etymology.story: Thalamos was the inner room of a Greek house.

info.explanation: A shallow groove on the wall of the third ventricle separating the thalamus above from the hypothalamus below.

etymology.story: It was once thought to drain brain phlegm into the nose. Hypophysis means an undergrowth, as it hangs below the brain.

info.explanation: The master endocrine gland hanging from the hypothalamus by the pituitary stalk, with an anterior (adenohypophysis) and posterior (neurohypophysis) lobe.

facts.function: Secretes hormones that control other endocrine glands

etymology.story: Early stains showed this glial cell with few short processes.

info.explanation: The glial cell that myelinates CNS axons, with one cell wrapping segments of several axons. (Schwann cells myelinate in the PNS.)

facts.function: CNS myelin formation

etymology.literal: cortex in front of the frontal (motor) areas
etymology.story: It lies rostral to the premotor and motor cortex.

info.explanation: Cortex at the front of the frontal lobe, including dorsolateral, orbitofrontal and ventromedial parts, supporting executive function, planning and social behavior.

facts.function: Executive function, planning, decision making, emotional regulation

etymology.story: Occiput is from ob (behind) plus caput (head).

info.explanation: A small indentation on the inferolateral surface of the hemisphere near the occipital pole, used as a landmark to mark the border between the temporal and occipital lobes.

etymology.story: The bony spiral cavity resembles a snail shell.

info.explanation: The coiled, fluid-filled inner ear structure whose hair cells transduce sound into neural signals carried by the cochlear division of CN VIII toward primary auditory cortex.

facts.function: Auditory transduction

roots.meaning: to disregard (nec, not + legere, to pick up)

etymology.story: Patients ignore half of space or their own body.

info.explanation: A syndrome in which a patient fails to attend to one side of space, classically the left after a right parietal lesion.

facts.lesion: Typically right parietal lobe damage producing left-sided neglect

etymology.story: Lies behind the postcentral gyrus.

info.explanation: The sulcus forming the posterior border of the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex), separating it from the superior parietal lobule.

etymology.story: Named for its supposed resemblance to a cuckoo's beak.

info.explanation: The coccyx is the small fused terminal part of the vertebral column below the sacrum, made of about four rudimentary vertebrae (Co1-Co4).

roots.meaning: the Titan condemned to hold up the sky

etymology.story: The first cervical vertebra holds up the skull like Atlas holding up the heavens.

info.explanation: The atlas is the C1 vertebra. It has no vertebral body and carries the skull at the atlanto-occipital joint (nodding).

etymology.story: The atlas turns about the dens of C2 as on an axle.

info.explanation: The axis is the C2 vertebra. Its dens (odontoid process) is the pivot around which the atlas and skull rotate.

etymology.story: C7 has a long spinous process that can be felt as a bump at the base of the neck.

info.explanation: The vertebra prominens is C7, identified by its long, easily palpated spinous process; it is a surface landmark for counting vertebral levels.

etymology.story: Latin costa gives English words such as costal.

info.explanation: The ribs are the 12 pairs of curved bones that articulate with the thoracic vertebrae and, with the sternum, form the rib cage protecting the thoracic organs.

etymology.story: A rootlet is a small filament; several rootlets merge to form a root.

info.explanation: Rootlets are the small filaments that emerge from the spinal cord (dorsal and ventral) and converge to form the dorsal and ventral roots of a spinal nerve.

etymology.story: Spinal nerves 'root' in the cord like a plant in soil.

info.explanation: Each spinal nerve forms from a dorsal (sensory) root and a ventral (motor) root, each made of converging rootlets; the roots unite in the intervertebral foramen.

etymology.story: The dura mater (tough mother) forms a tube-like bag around the cord and CSF.

info.explanation: The dural sac is the dura-lined sac containing the spinal cord, cauda equina and CSF; it ends around S2 below the conus medullaris.

etymology.story: From Latin proximus, superlative of prope 'near'.

info.explanation: Proximal describes a position closer to the trunk or point of attachment, for example the shoulder is proximal to the elbow.

etymology.story: Related to English distant.

info.explanation: Distal describes a position farther from the trunk or point of attachment, for example the hand is distal to the elbow.

roots.meaning: spinel, a tool for spinning thread

etymology.story: Muscle was named for a rippling muscle that looked like a mouse under the skin; the receptor is spindle-shaped.

info.explanation: Muscle spindles are stretch receptors within muscle that signal muscle length and its rate of change (proprioception, Ia and II afferents).

facts.function: proprioception of muscle length

roots.meaning: surname of Camillo Golgi, who described it

etymology.story: Named for Camillo Golgi, who described it in tendons.

info.explanation: The Golgi tendon organ sits at the muscle-tendon junction and signals muscle tension (Ib afferents), giving proprioceptive feedback and protecting against excess force.

facts.function: proprioception of muscle tension

etymology.story: It looks as if it has one process, but that process splits in two.

info.explanation: Primary sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglion are pseudounipolar: a single process leaves the soma and divides into a peripheral and a central branch.

etymology.story: From ipse plus lateral.

info.explanation: Ipsilateral means on the same side of the body or midline; for example dorsal column fibers ascend ipsilaterally until they decussate in the medulla.

etymology.story: Greek arteria first meant windpipe; the ancients thought arteries carried air.

info.explanation: The PICA arises from the vertebral artery and supplies the inferior cerebellum and the lateral medulla.

facts.lesion: lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome

name: Aneurysm
region: Cerebral arteries (often at branch points of the circle of Willis)

etymology.story: From Greek aneurysma, a widening, from aneurynein, to dilate. A berry aneurysm is a small sac that bulges like a berry from an artery wall.

info.explanation: An aneurysm is a weakened, ballooned arterial wall. A ruptured berry aneurysm bleeds into the subarachnoid space (subarachnoid hemorrhage), and treatment includes surgical clipping or endovascular platinum coils.

facts.lesion: Rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage, with a sudden severe headache.

etymology.story: The name gives the position of the nucleus within the thalamus: ventral, posterior and lateral.

info.explanation: The VPL relays body somatosensation from the medial lemniscus and the anterolateral system to the primary somatosensory cortex. Second-order neurons of the medial lemniscus synapse here, and the third-order neurons have their cell bodies here.

facts.function: Body touch, vibration, proprioception, pain and temperature relay to cortex.
facts.connections: Input: medial lemniscus, anterolateral system. Output: postcentral gyrus.

etymology.story: It arises in the red nucleus (nucleus ruber) of the midbrain, named for its pinkish colour in fresh tissue, and runs to the spinal cord.

info.explanation: The rubrospinal tract arises from the red nucleus, crosses in the ventral tegmental decussation and descends in the lateral funiculus. It facilitates flexor muscles of the upper limb. It does not travel through the cerebral peduncles because it starts in the midbrain tegmentum.

facts.function: Flexion of upper limb.
facts.passes: Tegmentum of midbrain, pons and medulla, then lateral funiculus.
facts.lesion: Damage below the red nucleus leaves extensor drive unopposed (decerebrate posturing).
facts.connections: Red nucleus to spinal LMNs.

etymology.story: It starts in the tectum (roof) of the midbrain, the superior and inferior colliculi.

info.explanation: The tectospinal tract arises from the colliculi, crosses in the dorsal tegmental decussation and descends to cervical cord levels. It produces reflexive head turns toward visual and auditory stimuli.

facts.function: Reflex orientation of head and neck toward visual and auditory stimuli.
facts.connections: Superior and inferior colliculi to cervical spinal LMNs.

etymology.story: Vestibulum is Latin for entrance hall, applied to the inner ear chamber that senses head position.

info.explanation: The vestibulospinal tract arises from the vestibular nuclei and descends ipsilaterally to facilitate extensor muscles of the trunk and limbs. It maintains posture and balance.

facts.function: Posture and balance via extensor tone.
facts.connections: Vestibular nuclei to spinal LMNs (ipsilateral).

etymology.story: The reticular formation is a netlike mix of cells and fibres in the brainstem core.

info.explanation: The reticulospinal tracts arise from the pontine and medullary reticular formation and modulate posture, muscle tone and locomotion, including rhythmic stepping. Regulation of voluntary fine movement belongs to the corticospinal system.

facts.function: Posture, tone, walking and gait, autonomic modulation.
facts.connections: Reticular formation to spinal interneurons and LMNs.

etymology.story: Bulb was an old term for the brainstem, so the tract runs from the cortex to the brainstem.

info.explanation: The corticobulbar tract is made of upper motor neuron axons that end on cranial nerve motor nuclei in the brainstem. This distinguishes it from the corticospinal tract, which ends in the spinal cord.

facts.function: Voluntary control of face, jaw, tongue and pharynx muscles.
facts.connections: Motor cortex via genu of internal capsule to cranial motor nuclei.

etymology.story: It links the cortex to the pontine nuclei in the basis pontis.

info.explanation: Corticopontine fibers carry copies of cortical motor plans to the pontine nuclei, which relay them across the middle cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral cerebellum. Their neurons are cortical neurons projecting to brainstem targets, so they count as upper motor neurons.

facts.function: Relay of motor plans to the cerebellum.
facts.passes: Cerebral peduncle, basis pontis, middle cerebellar peduncle.
facts.connections: Cortex to pontine nuclei to contralateral cerebellum.

etymology.story: Greek arkhi- means first or chief; this is the oldest cortex phylogenetically.

info.explanation: The archicortex is the hippocampal cortex, a three-layered allocortex with fewer layers than the six-layered neocortex.

etymology.story: Greek allos means other; it differs from the six-layered neocortex.

info.explanation: Allocortex is cortex with three to five layers (fewer than six), and includes archicortex (hippocampus) and paleocortex (olfactory cortex).

etymology.story: Greek palaios means old; it is evolutionarily older than neocortex.

info.explanation: Paleocortex includes the olfactory cortex (piriform cortex) and has fewer than six layers, a type of allocortex.

etymology.story: Greek hydrokephalon meant water in the head, long before CSF was understood.

info.explanation: Hydrocephalus is excess CSF in the ventricles, from blocked flow or poor absorption, and it enlarges the ventricles. It differs from disorders of neuronal migration, which are developmental malformations of the cortex.

facts.lesion: Raised intracranial pressure, enlarged head in infants.

etymology.story: It is a small sac in the membranous labyrinth.

info.explanation: The saccule and utricle are the otolith organs that detect linear acceleration and head tilt relative to gravity. The saccule is most sensitive to vertical linear acceleration, while the semicircular canals detect angular acceleration.

facts.function: Detects linear (vertical) acceleration.

roots.meaning: surname of Jan Evangelista Purkyne, who described these cells in 1837

etymology.story: Purkyne, a Czech anatomist and physiologist, first described them.

info.explanation: Purkinje cells are the only output neurons of the cerebellar cortex. They are GABAergic and inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei, which is how the cerebellar cortex modulates cerebellar output.

facts.function: Inhibitory output of cerebellar cortex.
facts.connections: Purkinje cells to deep cerebellar nuclei.

etymology.story: The two Greek roots combine directly, with kinesis from kinein, to move.

info.explanation: Bradykinesia is the slowness of movement that is a cardinal sign of Parkinson disease, due to loss of dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra, which reduces drive through the direct pathway.

facts.lesion: Parkinson disease, with rigidity and resting tremor.

etymology.literal: image of the spread of water
etymology.story: It measures how water diffuses in tissue along many directions.

info.explanation: DSI is a type of diffusion MRI that measures water diffusion in many directions and can resolve crossing fibre pathways, so it is suited to tracing complex axon tract crossings.

facts.function: Maps white matter tracts and fibre crossings.

etymology.literal: recording of slices by positive electron emission
etymology.story: A radiotracer emits positrons whose annihilation produces photons detected by the scanner.

info.explanation: PET uses radiolabeled tracers (for example FDG for metabolism, or labeled tau or amyloid) to image function and molecular targets. It is used for metabolic activity and for detecting tau aggregates in Alzheimer disease.

facts.function: Metabolic and molecular imaging.

etymology.literal: injury of the upper movers' nerve cells
etymology.story: Upper motor neurons are the cortical and brainstem cells that command the lower motor neurons, so damage is upstream of the final pathway.

info.explanation: Damage to cortical or descending motor neurons (corticospinal, corticobulbar) causes spastic paralysis: weakness with increased tone, brisk reflexes and an upgoing toe (Babinski sign). The lower motor neurons are intact, so there is no major atrophy.

facts.lesion: Spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, little atrophy

etymology.literal: injury of the lower movers' nerve cells
etymology.story: Lower motor neurons (ventral horn and cranial motor nuclei) are the final common path to muscle.

info.explanation: Damage to ventral horn cells, ventral roots or peripheral nerves causes flaccid paralysis with low tone, absent reflexes, fasciculations and muscle atrophy, because muscle loses its direct neural drive.

facts.lesion: Flaccid paralysis, areflexia, fasciculations, atrophy

etymology.story: Each dermatome is the strip of skin supplied by one spinal nerve root.

info.explanation: A dermatome is the area of skin innervated by the sensory fibers of a single dorsal root (spinal level). Lesions of a dorsal root or ganglion cause numbness in the matching strip, which helps localize the level.

facts.lesion: Numbness in a strip of skin matching the damaged root

etymology.story: The macula is the small central retinal spot of sharpest vision; in some cortical strokes it survives.

info.explanation: In a posterior cerebral artery stroke with homonymous hemianopia, central (macular) vision is often preserved, commonly attributed to dual supply of the occipital pole from the MCA as well as the PCA.

facts.supply: Occipital pole may have collateral MCA supply in addition to PCA

etymology.literal: the nucleus in the belly-side, behind and toward the middle
etymology.story: Named for its position in the ventral tier of the thalamus, behind and medial to VPL.

info.explanation: The thalamic relay for somatosensation from the face: it receives the trigeminal lemniscus and trigeminothalamic tract and projects to the face area of primary somatosensory cortex.

facts.function: Relays facial touch, pain and temperature to the cortex.
facts.connections: Input: trigeminal pathways. Output: primary somatosensory cortex (face area).

etymology.literal: nerve terminals without an encapsulated receptor
etymology.story: They are bare axon terminals, in contrast to encapsulated receptors such as Pacinian corpuscles.

info.explanation: Unencapsulated terminals of A-delta and C fibers that detect painful, thermal and itch stimuli and feed the anterolateral system.

etymology.story: Greek sympatheia 'feeling with'; early anatomists thought this system linked the organs so they 'felt with' each other.

info.explanation: The thoracolumbar division of the autonomic system (preganglionic cell bodies in the lateral horn, T1-L2) with short preganglionic and long postganglionic fibers; it mobilises the body for fight or flight.

facts.function: Fight or flight responses.

etymology.story: Named for lying alongside and opposing the sympathetic division.

info.explanation: The craniosacral division of the autonomic system (CN III, VII, IX, X and sacral S2-S4) with long preganglionic and short postganglionic fibers whose ganglia lie near or in the target organ; it supports rest and digest functions.

facts.function: Rest and digest functions.

roots.meaning: vertebra, joint, from vertere, to turn

etymology.literal: knots beside or in front of the vertebrae
etymology.story: Chain (paravertebral) ganglia lie beside the vertebral column and prevertebral ganglia lie in front of it.

info.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic axons synapse in the paravertebral chain ganglia or in prevertebral ganglia, where postganglionic neurons begin the long fibers to the target.

etymology.literal: inner part of the gland near the kidney
etymology.story: The adrenal gland sits on top of the kidney; its core is the medulla.

info.explanation: A modified sympathetic ganglion: its chromaffin cells are innervated directly by cholinergic preganglionic neurons and release epinephrine into the blood.

roots.meaning: spastikos, drawing in, from spaein, to pull

etymology.story: Greek spasmos meant a pulling or convulsion; paralysis comes from 'loosening' at the side.

info.explanation: The paralysis of upper motor neuron damage: increased tone, hyperreflexia and a Babinski sign without marked atrophy, because lower motor neurons remain intact and lose descending inhibition.

etymology.story: Latin flaccus, hanging loose, describes the limp muscle.

info.explanation: The paralysis of lower motor neuron damage: reduced tone, absent reflexes and muscle atrophy, because the muscle has lost its direct motor innervation.

etymology.story: Trigeminus, 'triplet', names the nerve for its three divisions (V1, V2, V3).

info.explanation: Its pseudounipolar neurons are the first-order cell bodies for facial touch, pain and temperature; it lies in the middle cranial fossa (Meckel's cave).

etymology.literal: tract from the trigeminal nuclei to the thalamus
etymology.story: Named by origin and destination, like spinothalamic.

info.explanation: Carries second-order facial pain and temperature fibers from the spinal trigeminal nucleus, crossing to the contralateral side and ending in VPM, alongside the anterolateral system.

name: Mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve

etymology.story: Mesencephalon, 'midbrain', is where this column lies.

info.explanation: It contains first-order proprioceptive neurons from the muscles of mastication whose cell bodies sit inside the CNS rather than in a ganglion; their axons synapse on the motor trigeminal nucleus for the jaw jerk reflex.

facts.function: Proprioception from chewing muscles; jaw reflex.

etymology.story: Named as if the cortex were removed, though the lesion is above the red nucleus rather than the cortex alone.

info.explanation: Flexed arms and extended legs after a lesion above the red nucleus: the rubrospinal tract is intact and drives upper limb flexion, while the lateral corticospinal tract is lost.

etymology.story: Named from animal experiments in which the cerebrum was removed.

info.explanation: Extended arms and legs after a lesion below the red nucleus: the rubrospinal tract is lost and pontine reticulospinal and vestibulospinal extensor drive is unopposed.

etymology.story: Defined in relation to the medullary pyramids, which carry the corticospinal tract.

info.explanation: Descending motor pathways other than the corticospinal tract (rubrospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, tectospinal), which arise in the brainstem.

etymology.story: Rods and cones are named for the shapes of their outer segments.

info.explanation: The retinal cells that transduce light. Rods work in dim light; cones give colour and acuity in bright light. They synapse on bipolar cells, which synapse on ganglion cells.

etymology.story: Called the 'what' pathway because it identifies objects.

info.explanation: The cortical visual route from primary visual cortex into the inferior temporal lobe that handles object and face recognition.

etymology.story: Called the 'where' pathway because it processes spatial position and motion.

info.explanation: The cortical visual route from primary visual cortex into the parietal lobe that handles spatial vision and visually guided movement.

etymology.literal: nucleus in front of the roof
etymology.story: It lies rostral to the superior colliculus (tectum).

info.explanation: Receives retinal input and projects bilaterally to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei, forming the central link of the pupillary light reflex.

facts.function: Pupillary light reflex.

etymology.literal: eye area of the forehead (frontal) lobe
etymology.story: Frontal comes from the Latin for forehead.

info.explanation: Cortex at Brodmann area 8 that drives voluntary contralateral saccades by way of the superior colliculus and the paramedian pontine reticular formation.

facts.function: Voluntary saccades.

etymology.story: It winds in the modiolus of the coiled cochlea.

info.explanation: Its bipolar neurons are the first-order cells of the cochlear nerve; peripheral processes contact hair cells and central axons enter the cochlear nuclei.

etymology.story: The vestibule of the inner ear gave the system its name.

info.explanation: Medullary and pontine nuclei that receive the vestibular nerve and project to the cerebellum, the MLF (eye movements) and the vestibulospinal tract.

etymology.story: Named for the snail-shaped cochlea of the inner ear, whose nerve ends here.

info.explanation: Dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei on the lateral surface of the rostral medulla at the pontomedullary junction, draped over the inferior cerebellar peduncle. They receive the cochlear nerve and are the first synapse of the auditory pathway, projecting mainly contralaterally (trapezoid body, superior olive, lateral lemniscus) to the inferior colliculus.

etymology.story: Named for the dense, grain-like appearance of the small cell bodies in the granular layer.

info.explanation: Cerebellar granule cells receive mossy fibers and send parallel fibers that excite Purkinje cells.

etymology.story: It lies between the fastigial and dentate nuclei.

info.explanation: Comprises the emboliform and globose nuclei, receives the paravermis and projects through the superior cerebellar peduncle to the red nucleus and thalamus for distal limb control.

name: Ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei

etymology.literal: nuclei in the front and side of the ventral tier
etymology.story: Named by position within the ventral nuclear group.

info.explanation: The motor thalamic relays: VA receives basal ganglia (GPi) output and VL receives cerebellar output, and both project to motor cortical areas.

name: Direct pathway of the basal ganglia

etymology.story: Called direct because the striatum inhibits GPi in a single step, with no intervening nucleus.

info.explanation: D1-bearing striatal neurons inhibit GPi, which disinhibits the thalamus and excites motor cortex, promoting movement ('go').

name: Indirect pathway of the basal ganglia

etymology.story: Called indirect because the route passes through GPe and the subthalamic nucleus before reaching GPi.

info.explanation: D2-bearing striatal neurons inhibit GPe, which disinhibits STN; STN excites GPi, which inhibits the thalamus and suppresses movement ('no-go').

roots.meaning: olfacere, to smell (olere, to emit smell + facere, to make)

etymology.story: Epithelium was coined for tissue covering the nipple, later any covering tissue.

info.explanation: The roof of the nasal cavity where bipolar olfactory receptor neurons, the first-order cells of smell, are renewed throughout life and send axons through the cribriform plate.

etymology.story: The plate is perforated like a sieve by olfactory axon bundles.

info.explanation: The part of the ethmoid bone forming the floor of the anterior cranial fossa through which olfactory nerve filaments pass; fracture can cause anosmia.

etymology.story: Its swollen, rounded shape resembles a bulb.

info.explanation: Where olfactory axons synapse on mitral cells, the second-order neurons whose axons form the olfactory tract.

etymology.story: Tract means a bundle of fibers running a common course.

info.explanation: Carries mitral cell axons from the olfactory bulb to the primary olfactory cortex (olfactory tubercle, piriform cortex, amygdala) without a thalamic relay.

etymology.story: Named for the pear-like shape of the region at the temporal pole.

info.explanation: The principal primary olfactory cortex, receiving the olfactory tract directly; it is also called prepiriform cortex.

etymology.literal: nucleus of the middle and back
etymology.story: Named for its medial and dorsal position in the thalamus.

info.explanation: Reciprocally connected with the prefrontal cortex; in smell it relays olfactory cortex to orbitofrontal cortex for conscious odor perception.

etymology.story: It runs along the groove between the caudate and thalamus, forming the boundary of the lateral ventricle floor.

info.explanation: The main efferent bundle of the amygdala, curving along the caudate to the hypothalamus and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis.

name: Bed nucleus of the stria terminalis

etymology.literal: nucleus lying along the stria terminalis
etymology.story: The nucleus is a 'bed' of cells along the stria.

info.explanation: A basal forebrain nucleus within the extended amygdala that receives amygdala output via the stria terminalis and relays to hypothalamus and brainstem, linked to anxiety and stress.

etymology.story: The tegmentum is the 'covering' of the midbrain beneath the tectum.

info.explanation: Midbrain source of the mesolimbic dopamine projection to nucleus accumbens, central to reward and motivation.

etymology.story: Named for its medial position through the lateral hypothalamus into the forebrain.

info.explanation: Connects the brainstem and ventral tegmental area with the hypothalamus and basal forebrain, carrying dopaminergic, serotonergic and noradrenergic fibers of the reward system.
